At 18, she published two young adult novels, *Bewitched* and *Seduced by Fame*, with her mother's help. Her breakthrough came in 1994 when she landed the role of Shannon Reed in the Australian soap opera *Home and Away*, a character who struggles with anorexia. Her performance earned her two Logie Award nominations: Most Popular New Talent in 1995 and Most Popular Actress in 1997.

After leaving *Home and Away*, Fisher attended L'École Internationale de Théâtre Jacques Lecoq in Paris, studying clown, mime, and commedia dell'arte. She then appeared in British pantomime, toured with Darren Day in *Summer Holiday*, and played a role in the London production of *Così*. She also starred in the German slasher film *Swimming Pool* (2001).

Fisher transitioned to Hollywood in 2002 with a supporting role in *Scooby-Doo*, playing the love interest of Shaggy Rogers. Though the film received mixed reviews, it was a commercial success. She followed this with roles in the Australian comedy *The Wannabes* (2003) and the independent film *Dallas 362* (2003). Her performance in *The Wannabes* was praised for its charm, while her role in *I Heart Huckabees* (2004) was described as a "punchy little part."

Her breakthrough in Hollywood came with *Wedding Crashers* (2005), where she played the sexually aggressive younger daughter of a politician. The film was a critical and commercial success, earning her the MTV Movie Award for Best Breakthrough Performance. She then starred in *London* (2005), *Wedding Daze* (2006), *The Lookout* (2007), and *Hot Rod* (2007). Her role in *The Lookout* was particularly noted for her decision to portray her character as a victim of her own kindness rather than a typical femme fatale.

Fisher's first leading role was in *Confessions of a Shopaholic* (2009), where she played a shopping-addicted financial journalist. Despite mixed reviews, the film was a box office success. She continued with voice roles in *Horton Hears a Who!* (2008) and *Rango* (2011), the latter earning her an Alliance of Women Film Journalists Award.

In 2013, Fisher achieved mainstream recognition with roles in *The Great Gatsby* and *Now You See Me*. In *The Great Gatsby*, she played a brief but memorable role as a social climber, while in *Now You See Me*, she portrayed a stage magician. Both films were commercial hits. She also appeared in the fourth and fifth seasons of *Arrested Development* as an actress, earning a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination with the ensemble cast.

From 2015–2016, Fisher starred in *Visions* (2015), a horror film, and the action comedies *Grimsby* and *Keeping Up with the Joneses* (both 2016). She also voiced the Tooth Fairy in *Rise of the Guardians* (2012) and appeared in *Tag* (2018) and *The Beach Bum* (2019).

In addition to acting, Fisher has written the *Marge in Charge* book series for children. She was married to English comedian Sacha Baron Cohen from 2010 until his death in 2025, with whom she had three children. Fisher has maintained a successful career in both film and television, balancing Hollywood roles with voice acting and writing. Her work has been praised for its versatility, and she continues to be a prominent figure in the entertainment industry.

title: Harry Cave
text:
Henry Butler Cave, known as Harry Cave, was a prominent New Zealand cricketer who played a significant role in the country’s early Test cricket history. Born on 10 October 1922 in the Wanganui area, he came from a farming family with a strong cricketing background. His father ran a farm at Westmere, and his uncle, Ken Cave, umpired all four matches of New Zealand’s first Test series in 1929–30. After attending Westmere School and Wanganui Collegiate School, Cave took up farming, a profession that would often compete with his cricket career.

Cave was an all-rounder, standing six feet two inches tall, and was known for his accurate medium-pace bowling and middle-to-lower-order batting. He began playing for Wanganui in his teens and became a key player in the Hawke Cup. His first-class debut came with Wellington on Christmas Eve 1945. In January 1947, he took 6 for 44 in the first innings and 2 for 72 in the second, helping Wellington defeat Canterbury in the Plunket Shield. A torn elbow muscle in 1947 altered his bowling style, shifting his reliance from out-swingers to seamers, cutters, and in-swingers.

In 1949, Cave was selected for New Zealand’s tour of England, playing in all four Tests. While Wisden described his bowling as "steady and reliable," the favorable batting conditions limited his success, with only four wickets in 141 overs at an average of 116.25. His domestic career flourished in the early 1950s, particularly with Central Districts, which joined the Plunket Shield in 1950–51. In 1952–53, he and Ian Leggat set a New Zealand ninth-wicket record with 239 runs, a partnership that still stands. Later that season, he took 13 wickets in a single day—7 for 31 and 6 for 33—against Auckland, securing a decisive victory.

Cave’s leadership skills were recognized when he became Central Districts’ captain in 1953–54, leading them to their first Plunket Shield title. He also topped the competition’s bowling averages with 24 wickets at 15.50. After a five-year Test absence, he returned for the 1954–55 series against England and was subsequently appointed captain for New Zealand’s grueling 1955–56 tour of Pakistan and India. The tour was marked by extreme heat, poor facilities, unfamiliar pitches, and health issues, but Cave remained composed, bowling 333 overs for 13 wickets. He lost significant weight and took two years to recover.

Upon returning, Cave captained New Zealand in the First Test against the West Indies but missed the Second. He returned for the Third and Fourth Tests, where he played under John Reid’s captaincy. In the Fourth Test, he delivered his best Test performance, taking 8 for 129 in the match to help New Zealand secure its first-ever Test victory. His match figures of 40.4–26–43–8 included the decisive wicket of Alf Valentine, stumped by Sammy Guillen.

In 1956–57, Cave was New Zealand’s leading bowler against Australia, taking 17 wickets in three unofficial Tests, while his teammates collectively took 17. In 1958, he toured England as vice-captain to John Reid, but the trip was unremarkable, with limited Test appearances and modest returns.

Off the field, Cave married Vonnie Anderson in 1951, and they had two sons. The couple was passionate about camellia cultivation, and Cave developed a variety named after him. He died in Wanganui on 15 September 1989. Vonnie was later honored as a Member of the New Zealand Order of Merit for her contributions to photography and horticulture, and she passed away in 2021.

title: Thierry Henry
text:
Thierry Henry, born on 17 August 1977 in Les Ulis, a suburb of Paris, is widely regarded as one of the greatest footballers of all time and the finest player in Premier League history. Known for his finishing, dribbling, speed, and chance-creating abilities, Henry was a prolific goalscorer and a key playmaker throughout his career. He was a two-time runner-up for both the Ballon d'Or (2003) and FIFA World Player of the Year (2003, 2004). His individual accolades include being named the FWA Footballer of the Year three times, a joint-record two PFA Players' Player of the Year awards, and six consecutive inclusions in the PFA Team of the Year. He was also part of the FIFA FIFPro World XI and the UEFA Team of the Year five times. In 2004, Pelé included him in the FIFA 100 list of the world's greatest living players.

Henry began his professional career at Monaco in 1994, where he quickly impressed, helping the club win Ligue 1 and reaching the UEFA Champions League semi-finals. After a brief and unsuccessful stint at Juventus in 1999, he joined Arsenal for £11 million. Under manager Arsène Wenger, Henry flourished, becoming Arsenal's all-time leading scorer with 228 goals across all competitions. He won the Premier League Golden Boot four times, two Premier League titles, and three FA Cups. His peak came during the 2003–04 season when Arsenal went unbeaten to win the league, and Henry set a record for most assists in a Premier League season (23) while also scoring 24 goals. He captained Arsenal in his final years, leading them to the 2006 UEFA Champions League Final before leaving for Barcelona in 2007.

At Barcelona, Henry was part of the 2008–09 treble-winning team, securing La Liga, the Copa del Rey, and the UEFA Champions League. In 2010, he moved to Major League Soccer (MLS) with the New York Red Bulls, briefly returning to Arsenal on loan in 2012 before retiring in 2014.

Henry's international career with France was equally decorated. He won the 1998 FIFA World Cup, UEFA Euro 2000, and the 2003 FIFA Confederations Cup, where he was awarded the Golden Ball and Golden Shoe. He became France's record goalscorer in 2007, a record he held until 2022. After 123 appearances and 51 goals, he retired from international football in 2010.

Post-retirement, Henry transitioned into coaching. He worked with Arsenal's youth teams and as a pundit for Sky Sports before becoming an assistant coach for Belgium in 2016. In 2018, he took over as head coach of Monaco but was dismissed in 2019. He then managed the Montréal Impact (now CF Montréal) in MLS, leading them to the playoffs in 2020. He returned as an assistant coach for Belgium before managing France's under-21 and Olympic teams, guiding the latter to a silver medal at the 2024 Summer Games.

Henry's career was defined by his electrifying skill, consistency, and leadership, leaving an indelible mark on both club and international football.

title: Andriy Yarmolenko
text:
Andriy Mykolayovych Yarmolenko, born on 23 October 1989 in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg), is a Ukrainian professional footballer who plays as a winger or forward for Dynamo Kyiv and captains the Ukraine national team. His parents, originally from Smolianka village in Chernihiv Oblast, returned to Ukraine when he was three years old, settling in Chernihiv. Yarmolenko began playing football at a young age, initially with a self-made ball due to his family's financial struggles. He was later scouted by Mykola Lypoviy and joined the Youth Sports School "Yunist" in Chernihiv.

Yarmolenko's professional career began with Yunist Chernihiv before moving to Dynamo Kyiv's youth academy at age 13, though he returned to Chernihiv after struggling to meet physical demands. In 2006, he joined Desna Chernihiv, where he scored four goals in nine appearances in the Ukrainian First League. In 2007, he signed a five-year contract with Dynamo Kyiv, initially playing for their second team before debuting for the first team in May 2008. He quickly established himself as a key player, scoring seven goals in his first season and earning comparisons to Andriy Shevchenko. Over his time with Dynamo, he won multiple Ukrainian Premier League titles, Ukrainian Cups, and Ukrainian Super Cups, becoming a top scorer and multiple-time Ukrainian Footballer of the Year.

In 2017, Yarmolenko moved to Borussia Dortmund but struggled to secure a regular starting spot. The following year, he joined West Ham United, where he became a fan favorite, scoring crucial goals, including a winner against Chelsea in July 2020. His tenure was marked by injuries, including an Achilles tear in 2018 and an adductor muscle tear in 2019. Despite these setbacks, he contributed significantly, such as scoring in the Europa League round of 16 against Sevilla in 2022, helping West Ham reach the quarterfinals for the first time in over 40 years.

In 2022, Yarmolenko briefly moved to Al-Ain in the United Arab Emirates before returning to Dynamo Kyiv in 2023. His international career for Ukraine is equally distinguished, debuting in 2009 and becoming a key player, scoring 46 goals in 125 matches. He has represented Ukraine in multiple UEFA European Championships (2012, 2016, 2020, 2024) and holds the record for the fastest goal in Ukraine's history, scoring 14 seconds into a match against Uruguay in 2011. He also played a pivotal role in Ukraine's 2016 Euro qualification, scoring in both legs of the playoff against Slovenia.

Beyond football, Yarmolenko is known for his humanitarian efforts, particularly during the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. He donated £75,000 to the Ukrainian Armed Forces, helped evacuate civilians from Chernihiv, and donated an ambulance to his hometown. He has also been honored as an honorary citizen of Chernihiv and has three sons with his wife, Inna.

Yarmolenko's achievements include being named Ukrainian Footballer of the Year in 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2017, as well as multiple domestic accolades. In September 2024, he obtained a UEFA "A" coaching license, hinting at a future in coaching. His legacy extends beyond his on-field success, encompassing his leadership, resilience, and contributions to Ukraine both on and off the pitch.

title: Gary Woodland
text:
Gary Woodland is an American professional golfer born on May 21, 1984, in Topeka, Kansas. He gained prominence in the sport, particularly after winning the U.S. Open in 2019, his first major championship and sixth professional victory. Woodland’s early life was marked by a transition from basketball to golf. After attending Shawnee Heights High School, he initially played basketball on a scholarship at Washburn University before transferring to the University of Kansas on a golf scholarship. There, he studied sociology and achieved success as an amateur golfer, winning four tournaments before turning professional in 2007.

Woodland’s early professional career was challenging. He played on the Nationwide Tour in 2007 and 2008 before securing his PGA Tour card by finishing tied for 11th at the Qualifying School in 2008. However, his debut PGA Tour season in 2009 was difficult, as he made only eight cuts in 18 events before a shoulder injury ended his season. In 2010, he split time between the PGA and Nationwide Tours, failing to secure a top-10 finish but finishing 92nd on the Nationwide Tour money list. He re-entered the Qualifying School at the end of the year and again earned a PGA Tour card by finishing tied for 11th.

Woodland’s breakthrough came in 2011 when he won his first PGA Tour event, the Transitions Championship, by one stroke over Webb Simpson. This victory elevated him to 53rd in the Official World Golf Ranking and earned him invitations to major tournaments, including the Masters and U.S. Open. Later that year, he teamed with Matt Kuchar to win the Omega Mission Hills World Cup. By the end of 2011, he had risen to 17th on the PGA Tour money list and 51st in the world rankings, a dramatic improvement from his previous standings.

In 2015, Woodland reached the final of the WGC-Cadillac Match Play, losing to Rory McIlroy but achieving a career-best 32nd in the world rankings. His next significant win came in February 2018 at the Waste Management Phoenix Open, where he defeated Chez Reavie in a sudden-death playoff. This victory moved him to fifth in the FedEx Cup standings. Later that year, he held the 36-hole lead at the PGA Championship, setting a tournament record with a 130 total through the first two rounds, but finished tied for sixth.

Woodland’s most notable achievement came in 2019 at the U.S. Open, where he held the 54-hole lead at Pebble Beach. He shot a final-round 69 to win by three strokes over Brooks Koepka, becoming the fourth U.S. Open champion to finish double-digits under par. The victory was his first major and moved him to 12th in the world rankings. Woodland’s win was particularly emotional, as he had previously invited Amy Bockerstette, a collegiate golfer with Down syndrome, to play with him during a practice round at the Waste Management Phoenix Open. Her par on a difficult hole in front of a cheering crowd went viral, and Woodland later credited her positive energy for his success. After his U.S. Open win, he FaceTimed Bockerstette and reunited with her on *The Today Show*, presenting her with a replica trophy.

That year, Woodland also represented the U.S. at the Presidents Cup, contributing to the team’s 16–14 victory, though he went 1–2–1 in his matches. In 2023, he faced a significant health challenge when he was diagnosed with a brain lesion, undergoing surgery in September. His resilience led to him being awarded the PGA Tour Courage Award in February 2025.

Woodland’s amateur career was also successful, with wins at events like the Cleveland State Invitational, Kansas Amateur, Kansas Invitational, All-American Golf Classic, and Louisiana Classics. As a professional, he has four PGA Tour victories, including the 2019 U.S. Open, and has represented the U.S. in international competitions. His journey from a struggling rookie to a major champion highlights his perseverance and skill in the sport.

title: James Theodore Bent
text:
James Theodore Bent (1852–1897) was an English explorer, archaeologist, and author, born in Liverpool to a wealthy family. His father, James Bent, was a brewer, and his grandfather, William Bent, founded Bent's Breweries, a business that supported the family's financial stability. Bent was educated at Malvern Wells, Repton School, and Wadham College, Oxford, graduating in 1875. In 1877, he married Mabel Hall-Dare, who became his travel companion, photographer, and diarist on his numerous expeditions.

Bent and his wife began their travels in 1877, visiting Italy and Greece annually. In 1879, he published *A Freak of Freedom*, a book about San Marino, and was granted citizenship there. The following year, he wrote *Genoa: How the Republic Rose and Fell* and, in 1881, a biography of Giuseppe Garibaldi. Their research in the Cyclades islands from 1882 to 1884 led to his book *The Cyclades; or, Life among the Insular Greeks* (1885).

From 1883 to 1888, Bent focused on archaeological and ethnographic work in the Eastern Mediterranean and Anatolia, contributing findings to journals such as the *Journal of Hellenic Studies*. His excavations on the Cycladic island of Antiparos were particularly notable. In 1889, he traveled to the Bahrein Islands in the Persian Gulf, searching for evidence of Phoenician civilization, and later met Shah Naser al-Din Shah Qajar in Persia. In 1890, he explored Cilicia Trachea, collecting valuable inscriptions.

One of Bent’s most significant contributions was his 1891 expedition to Mashonaland (modern-day Zimbabwe) with his wife and surveyor Robert McNair Wilson Swan. There, he conducted the first detailed study of Great Zimbabwe, arguing that the ruins were built by the ancestors of the Shona people. His findings were published in *The Ruined Cities of Mashonaland* (1892), though his conclusions were later disputed by scholars like Victor Loret and Alfred Foucher, who claimed a non-African origin. Modern archaeology now supports Bent’s theory.

In 1893, Bent explored the ruins of Axum in Ethiopia, documenting them in *The Sacred City of the Ethiopians* (1893). He later traveled to the Hadramut region of southern Arabia (1893–1894), studying its ancient history and identifying ruins along the Dhofar coast. In 1895–1896, he examined the African Red Sea coast, discovering evidence of ancient gold mines and Sabaean influence. During his final expedition to South Arabia and Socotra (1896–1897), Bent contracted malarial fever and died in London on 5 May 1897, shortly after returning.

Mabel Bent, who played a crucial role in his expeditions, published *Southern Arabia, Soudan and Sakotra* (1900), detailing their last journey. Bent’s extensive collections of artefacts are held in institutions like the British Museum, the Pitt Rivers Museum, and the Great Zimbabwe Museum. His scientific contributions include the naming of plant and animal species, such as *Echidnopsis Bentii* and *Uromastyx benti*. Some of his unpublished notebooks, held by the Hellenic Society, have been digitized and made publicly accessible.

title: Kajal Aggarwal
text:
Kajal Aggarwal, born on 19 June 1985 in Mumbai, is a prominent Indian actress known for her work in Telugu, Tamil, and Hindi films. She is widely regarded as one of the highest-paid actresses in South Indian cinema and has received numerous accolades, including three SIIMA Awards and four Filmfare Awards South nominations. Her career spans over two decades, marked by significant contributions to regional and Bollywood cinema.

Aggarwal began her acting journey with a minor role in the 2004 Hindi film *Kyun! Ho Gaya Na...*, playing Aishwarya Rai Bachchan's sister. She made her Telugu debut in 2007 with *Lakshmi Kalyanam*, but her breakthrough came the same year with *Chandamama*, which earned her critical recognition. However, her career truly took off with *Magadheera* (2009), a Telugu historical drama where she played dual roles. The film was a massive commercial success and earned her widespread acclaim, including a Filmfare Award nomination. It was later dubbed in Tamil as *Maaveeran* (2011), further expanding her reach.

Throughout the 2010s, Aggarwal established herself as a leading actress in Telugu and Tamil cinema. Some of her notable films include *Darling* (2010), *Brindavanam* (2010), *Mr. Perfect* (2011), *Businessman* (2012), *Naayak* (2013), *Baadshah* (2013), *Govindudu Andarivadele* (2014), *Temper* (2015), *Khaidi No. 150* (2017), and *Bhagavanth Kesari* (2023). In Tamil cinema, she starred in high-profile projects like *Naan Mahaan Alla* (2010), *Thuppakki* (2012), *Mersal* (2017), and *Comali* (2019). Her Hindi filmography includes *Singham* (2011) and *Special 26* (2013), which were well-received.

Aggarwal's performances have been praised for their versatility. Critics have often highlighted her ability to balance glamour with strong acting, particularly in films like *Magadheera*, *Naan Mahaan Alla*, and *Nene Raju Nene Mantri*. She has also been recognized for her chemistry with leading actors such as Ram Charan, Prabhas, and Vijay. In 2020, she became the first South Indian actress to have a wax figure at Madame Tussauds Singapore, underscoring her industry influence.

Born into a Punjabi family with roots in Amritsar, Aggarwal was raised in Mumbai. Her father, Vinay Aggarwal, is a textile entrepreneur, and her mother, Suman, is a confectioner and her business manager. She has a younger sister, Nisha Aggarwal, who is also an actress. Aggarwal pursued a degree in mass media with a specialization in marketing and advertising from Kishinchand Chellaram College and initially aspired to pursue an MBA.

In 2020, Aggarwal married Gautam Kitchlu in a private ceremony in Mumbai. The couple welcomed their son, Neil, in April 2022. Despite her personal commitments, she has continued to take on challenging roles in films like *Hey Sinamika* (2022) and *Sikandar* (2025). Upcoming projects include *Kannappa*, *Indian 3*, *The India Story*, and *Ramayana: Part 1*, where she will play Mandodari.

Aggarwal's journey from a debutant to a celebrated actress reflects her dedication to her craft. Her ability to navigate multiple film industries while maintaining a strong fan base is a testament to her talent and adaptability. As one of the most popular and influential actresses in South Indian cinema, she continues to inspire aspiring performers and leave a lasting impact on the film industry.

title: Vicente Guerrero
text:
Vicente Ramón Guerrero Saldaña (1782–1831) was a pivotal figure in Mexican history, serving as a revolutionary general and later the country’s second president. Born in Tixtla, near Acapulco, Guerrero hailed from a wealthy and influential family with ties to Spanish colonial authorities, yet he defied his father’s loyalty to Spain by joining the Mexican War of Independence in 1810. His early life as a muleteer exposed him to revolutionary ideas, and his ability to speak Spanish, Nahuatl, and other Indigenous languages earned him strong support among Mexico’s native populations.

Guerrero initially fought under José María Morelos, distinguishing himself in battles like Zitltala and Tixtla, where his knowledge of local languages and terrain proved invaluable. After Morelos’ execution in 1815, Guerrero continued the insurgency through guerrilla warfare, refusing a Spanish amnesty. By 1820, he allied with Agustín de Iturbide under the Plan of Iguala, which secured Mexico’s independence. The plan, influenced by Guerrero’s insistence, guaranteed equal rights for all Mexicans, regardless of race—a radical departure from Spain’s caste system.

Following Iturbide’s brief imperial rule, Guerrero became a key leader in the new republic, championing liberal causes as a member of the York Rite Masons. In the 1828 presidential election, despite losing the popular vote, Guerrero’s supporters—including military and political allies—forced the resignation of the elected president, Manuel Gómez Pedraza, allowing Guerrero to assume office on April 1, 1829, with Anastasio Bustamante as vice president.

Guerrero’s presidency was marked by reformist ideals, including the abolition of slavery (though Texas was later exempted to appease American settlers) and calls for public education, land reforms, and economic development. However, his administration faced internal strife, financial instability, and external threats from Spain. His mixed-race background and populist policies alienated conservative elites, and in 1830, Bustamante led a rebellion that deposed him. Guerrero was later captured and executed in 1831.

Despite his short presidency, Guerrero’s legacy endures as a champion of racial equality and social justice. His abolition of slavery and advocacy for Indigenous rights left a lasting mark on Mexican society, and his state, Guerrero, was named in his honor. His life reflects the complex struggles of Mexico’s transition from colonial rule to independence, embodying both the revolutionary spirit and the enduring challenges of nation-building.

title: Danny Faure
text:
Danny Faure, born on 8 May 1962, is a Seychellois politician who served as the fourth President of Seychelles from 16 October 2016 to 26 October 2020. Before assuming the presidency, he held the position of Vice-President from 2010 to 2016. A member of the United Seychelles Party (PP), Faure has had a long and varied political career, marked by his involvement in education, finance, and public administration.

Faure was born in Kilembe, a town in western Uganda, to Seychellois parents. He completed his primary and secondary education in the Seychelles before pursuing higher education at the University of Havana in Cuba, where he earned a degree in political science. His early professional life began in 1985 when, at the age of 23, he became an assistant curriculum officer at the Seychelles Ministry of Education. Concurrently, he worked as a lecturer at the National Youth Service and the Seychelles Polytechnic.

In 1993, following the reintroduction of multiparty democracy in Seychelles, Faure became the leader of government business in the National Assembly, a role he held until 1998. That same year, he was appointed Minister of Education, marking the start of his extensive ministerial career. Over the years, he held various key positions, including Minister of Youth, Minister of Finance, Minister of Trade and Industries, Minister of Public Administration, and Minister of Information and Communication Technology. His tenure as Minister of Finance, from 2006 to 2010, was particularly notable. Under his leadership, Seychelles implemented economic reforms recommended by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), with the first phase of these reforms running from October 2008 to October 2013. Faure also served as a designated minister from 2004 to 2010 before being appointed Vice-President in 2010, a role he retained while continuing to oversee the finance portfolio.

Faure’s presidency began unexpectedly when President James Michel announced his resignation on 27 September 2016, effective 16 October. The resignation came amid the election of an opposition majority in the National Assembly, and as vice president, Faure was sworn in to complete the remaining four years of Michel’s term. During his presidency, Faure made significant contributions to global environmental causes. In April 2019, he delivered a speech from an underwater research submersible, advocating for stronger protections for the world’s oceans. Later that year, in June 2019, he was recognized for his environmental advocacy when he received the National Geographic Society’s prestigious ‘Planetary and Leadership Award’ at George Washington University in Washington, D.C.

However, Faure’s political career came to an end in October 2020 when he lost the presidential election to Wavel Ramkalawan, who succeeded him as President of Seychelles. Beyond his political life, Faure is a family man, with four daughters and one son. In April 2021, he married Shermin Rudie Bastienne, marking a new chapter in his personal life.

Faure’s career reflects a dedication to public service, economic reform, and environmental advocacy, leaving a lasting impact on Seychelles and international environmental discourse.

title: Ilhan Omar
text:
Ilhan Omar is a prominent American politician serving as the U.S. representative for Minnesota's 5th congressional district since 2019. Born in Mogadishu, Somalia, on October 4, 1982, Omar fled the Somali Civil War with her family and spent four years in a Kenyan refugee camp before securing asylum in the U.S. in 1995. She settled in Minneapolis, where her father worked as a taxi driver and later for the post office. Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000 and graduated from North Dakota State University in 2011 with degrees in political science and international studies.

Before entering Congress, Omar worked as a community nutrition educator, campaign manager, and policy aide. In 2016, she was elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives, becoming the first Somali-American legislator in the U.S. Her tenure was marked by advocacy for progressive policies and controversy over campaign finance allegations, which were partly resolved with a fine and repayment of misused funds.

Omar was elected to Congress in 2018, making history as the first Somali-American in the U.S. House of Representatives, the first woman of color to represent Minnesota, and one of the first two Muslim women in Congress (alongside Rashida Tlaib). She has since become a leading progressive voice, serving as deputy chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and advocating for policies such as a $15 minimum wage, universal healthcare, student loan debt forgiveness, and the protection of DACA recipients. She also supports abolishing ICE and has been a vocal critic of Israel, endorsing the BDS movement and opposing pro-Israel lobbying groups. These positions have drawn criticism, including accusations of antisemitism, and in 2023, Republicans voted to remove her from the Foreign Affairs Committee.

During her time in Congress, Omar has introduced legislation on issues like student debt relief, school meal debt, and healthcare. She was part of the effort to impeach Donald Trump in 2021 and has been a prominent member of "The Squad," a group of progressive congresswomen pushing for policies like the Green New Deal and Medicare for All. Her tenure has been marked by significant media attention, with conservative outlets like Fox News frequently covering her, often critically.

Omar has faced personal challenges, including bullying during her youth and a violent attack during a political caucus. She has also been open about the trauma of the 2021 U.S. Capitol attack, describing her fear for her life during the evacuation. Throughout her career, she has remained a polarizing figure, with high approval among Democrats and strong disapproval among Republicans. Her reelection in 2024 secured her a fourth term, reinforcing her influence in national politics.

title: Nelson Mandela
text:
Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela, born on July 18, 1918, in the village of Mvezo in South Africa's Cape Province, was a Xhosa from the Thembu royal family. His name, Rolihlahla, means "troublemaker" in Xhosa, and he later became known by his clan name, Madiba. His father, Gadla Henry Mphakanyiswa Mandela, was a local chief and councillor, but he was dismissed from his position, leaving young Mandela to be raised by his mother and later the Thembu regent, Chief Jongintaba Dalindyebo. Mandela attended Methodist schools, where he was baptized and given the English name "Nelson" by his teacher. After his father’s death, he was sent to live with the regent and his family, where he received a formal education and developed a strong sense of justice.

Mandela began his secondary education at Clarkebury Methodist High School, where he excelled academically and socially. He later attended Healdtown Methodist College before enrolling at the University of Fort Hare, an elite institution for Black students. There, he befriended future ANC leader Oliver Tambo and participated in student activism, including a boycott that led to his suspension. After fleeing an arranged marriage, Mandela moved to Johannesburg in 1941, where he worked as a law clerk and continued his studies through correspondence courses.

In Johannesburg, Mandela became involved in anti-apartheid activism, joining the African National Congress (ANC) in 1943. He co-founded the ANC Youth League in 1944, advocating for African nationalism and resistance to white-minority rule. He married Evelyn Mase in 1944, and they had three children, though one died in infancy. Mandela studied law at the University of the Witwatersrand, facing racial discrimination but forming lifelong friendships with liberal and communist activists. Through the ANC Youth League, he worked to mobilize Black South Africans against apartheid, opposing alliances with non-Black groups and communists until later adopting a more inclusive approach.

As apartheid laws tightened under the National Party government, Mandela and the ANC escalated their resistance. He led the 1952 Defiance Campaign, a mass civil disobedience movement against apartheid laws, and co-organized the 1955 Congress of the People, which drafted the Freedom Charter, a foundational document for a non-racial South Africa. Mandela was repeatedly arrested and stood trial in the 1956 Treason Trial, though the charges were eventually dropped. Influenced by Marxist ideas, he secretly joined the South African Communist Party (SACP) and, in 1961, co-founded uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK), the ANC’s armed wing, which carried out sabotage campaigns against government targets.

In 1962, Mandela was arrested and sentenced to life imprisonment following the Rivonia Trial, where he delivered his famous "I am prepared to die" speech. He spent 27 years in prison, mostly on Robben Island, where he endured harsh conditions but continued to advocate for justice and reconciliation. As international and domestic pressure grew, President F.W. de Klerk released Mandela in 1990, leading to negotiations to end apartheid. In 1994, Mandela became South Africa’s first Black president in a fully democratic election, leading a government focused on racial reconciliation and drafting a new constitution. He established the Truth and Reconciliation Commission to address past human rights abuses and implemented policies to combat poverty and expand healthcare.

Mandela stepped down after one term, declining a second presidency, and became an elder statesman, advocating for global causes like HIV/AIDS awareness and poverty reduction. Despite criticism from both the right and the left, he was widely respected as a symbol of democracy and social justice, receiving over 250 honors, including the Nobel Peace Prize. He remained a beloved figure in South Africa, often called the "Father of the Nation." Mandela died on December 5, 2013, leaving a lasting legacy as a champion of freedom and equality.

title: Joey Jordison
text:
Nathan Jonas "Joey" Jordison was an American musician best known as the original drummer of the heavy metal band Slipknot, where he was designated as member #1. Born on April 26, 1975, in Des Moines, Iowa, Jordison developed an early interest in music, influenced by his parents, who encouraged him to listen to the radio rather than watch TV. He received his first drum kit at age eight and began playing in bands during his elementary school years. His parents' divorce and his mother's remarriage led him to take on responsibilities early in life, including helping at his stepfather's funeral parlor. Jordison's first notable band was Modifidious, a thrash metal group he formed in the early 1990s, which released several demos before disbanding.

In 1995, Jordison joined the Pale Ones, a band that would later evolve into Slipknot. He became the third member to join the group, which would go on to pioneer the new wave of American heavy metal. Slipknot's lineup, which included nine members from 1999 to 2010, featured Jordison as a key contributor, playing on their first five studio albums. He was also the producer of their 2005 live album, *9.0: Live*. Despite his success, Jordison faced health challenges, including a broken ankle in 2008 and a burst appendix in 2009, which forced the cancellation of several shows.

In December 2013, Slipknot announced Jordison's departure, citing personal reasons. Jordison later revealed that he had been fired and that he suffered from transverse myelitis, a neurological disease that eventually left him unable to play the drums. Before his departure, he had already begun working on other projects, including the horror punk band Murderdolls, which he co-founded in 2002 with Wednesday 13. The band released two albums and toured extensively before disbanding in 2011. After leaving Slipknot, Jordison formed Scar the Martyr in 2013, but the project ended in 2016. He also briefly worked on Vimic and joined the blackened death metal supergroup Sinsaenum, releasing two albums with them before his death.

Jordison was also known for his session work and touring appearances with major acts. In 2004, he filled in for Metallica drummer Lars Ulrich at the Download Festival, earning praise as the band's "hero of the day." He also toured with Ministry, Korn, Rob Zombie, and Satyricon. Additionally, he contributed to remixes and recordings for artists like Marilyn Manson, Otep, and Puscifer. Jordison's drumming style was influenced by legends like Neil Peart, Keith Moon, and John Bonham, and he was recognized for his skill, winning multiple awards, including Rhythm magazine's best drummer of the past 25 years in 2010.

Jordison's health struggles continued after his diagnosis of transverse myelitis, which left him temporarily unable to walk or play drums. He underwent rehabilitation and regained mobility, but his condition remained a challenge. On July 26, 2021, Jordison died in his sleep at the age of 46. Following his death, tributes poured in from musicians worldwide, and Slipknot dedicated their 2022 album *The End, So Far* in his memory. Jordison's legacy as a pioneering drummer and influential musician endures through his contributions to Slipknot and other bands, as well as his impact on the metal and punk scenes.

title: Ayman al-Zawahiri
text:
Ayman Mohammed Rabie al-Zawahiri (1951–2022) was an Egyptian-born militant Islamist leader who served as the second general emir of al-Qaeda from 2011 until his death in 2022. He was a central figure in planning the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and was known for his role in various high-profile attacks, including the 1998 U.S. embassy bombings in Kenya and Tanzania and the 2002 Bali bombings. Born into a wealthy and influential family in Giza, Egypt, on June 19, 1951, al-Zawahiri came from a background of scholars, politicians, and religious figures. His father was a surgeon and professor, while his mother’s family included prominent figures such as Abdel-Wahhab Azzam, a former president of Cairo University and founder of King Saud University, and Azzam Pasha, the first secretary-general of the Arab League. His uncle, Mahfouz Azzam, became a significant early influence, shaping his religious and political views.

Al-Zawahiri studied medicine at Cairo University, graduating in 1974 and later earning a master’s degree in surgery. He worked as a surgeon in the Egyptian Army and later ran a clinic. As a student, he was deeply influenced by the Islamist ideologue Sayyid Qutb, whose writings inspired his belief in establishing an Islamist state. By the age of 15, al-Zawahiri formed an underground cell aimed at overthrowing the Egyptian government. This group later merged with others to form the Egyptian Islamic Jihad (EIJ), of which he eventually became the leader.

In 1981, al-Zawahiri was arrested for his role in the assassination of Egyptian President Anwar Sadat. He was imprisoned until 1984, during which time he was reportedly tortured. After his release, he traveled to Pakistan, where he treated wounded Afghan refugees and met Osama bin Laden in 1986. He later moved to Saudi Arabia, where he practiced medicine in Jeddah before returning to the militant Islamist movement. In 1995, under his leadership, the EIJ carried out the bombing of the Egyptian embassy in Islamabad, Pakistan, though the operation was opposed by bin Laden.

Al-Zawahiri was sentenced to death in absentia by Egypt in 1999 for his role in anti-government attacks. He later merged the EIJ with al-Qaeda in 2001 and became bin Laden’s deputy in 2004. After bin Laden’s death in 2011, al-Zawahiri succeeded him as al-Qaeda’s leader. The U.S. government offered a $25 million reward for his capture, listing him as one of its most wanted terrorists.

Al-Zawahiri was married at least four times and had several children. His first wife, Azza Ahmed Nowari, and two of their children, including a son and a daughter with Down syndrome, were killed in a U.S. airstrike in Afghanistan in late 2001. He also played a role in directing the 2007 Lal Masjid siege in Pakistan, which resulted in over 100 deaths, and was implicated in the 2007 assassination of former Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto.

On July 31, 2022, al-Zawahiri was killed in a CIA drone strike in Afghanistan, ending his decades-long career as a key figure in global Islamist militancy. His death marked the end of a long-standing target for U.S. counterterrorism efforts.

title: Diego Suarez (garden designer)
text:
Diego Suarez (1888–1974), a renowned garden designer, was born in Bogotá, Colombia, to a diplomat and historian, Roberto Suarez, and his Italian wife, Maria Costa. After his father’s death, Suarez and his siblings—Camelia, Lucia, and Roberto—spent their childhood in Italy. He studied architectural design at the Accademia delle Belle Arti in Florence, where he was mentored by Arthur Acton, an English expatriate restoring the gardens of Villa La Pietra. Through Acton, Suarez was exposed to Renaissance garden ideals, which were being revived in the late 19th century by designers like Achille Duchêne. Acton introduced Suarez to the Anglo-American community in Florence, where he began designing gardens, including one at Villa Schifanoia for Lewis Einstein and another for Charles Loeser, an early collector of Paul Cézanne’s works.

In 1914, Suarez’s career took a significant turn when he was commissioned by Arthur Acton to show James Deering, the International Harvester heir, and his artistic advisor, Paul Chalfin, around Florence. This connection led to a pivotal opportunity: Lady Sybil Cutting, who owned the Villa Medici in Fiesole, suggested that Suarez accompany her to America. The outbreak of World War I stranded him in New York, where he maintained professional connections. It was through these ties that he was invited to design the gardens for Villa Vizcaya, Deering’s grand estate in Miami, Florida.

Villa Vizcaya’s gardens, completed under Suarez’s direction, became his most famous work. The design centered on two façades: one facing Biscayne Bay, featuring a boat-shaped central island with balustrades, obelisks, and tree-lined "bosquets" at the bow and stern, and another with a south-facing garden. The latter included a central axis leading to a casino, with side axes offering glimpses of the lake beyond. A key feature was the Bassano di Sutri fountain, which Deering believed was by Vignola. Suarez strategically placed it at the end of a cross-axis, ensuring it was discovered only after exploring the garden. The design incorporated French baroque parterres, sun-and-shade contrasts, and subtle changes in elevation to enhance the flat site’s visual interest.

Beyond Villa Vizcaya, Suarez’s career included diplomatic roles. He served as a press attaché and minister-counselor for Chile in Washington, D.C., from 1948 to 1952, and later as counselor to the Colombian delegation to the United Nations. In 1952, he collaborated with architect Frederic Rhinelander King to design a neoclassical house with extensive gardens in Brookville, New York.

Suarez married Evelyn Marshall Field in 1937 in Monterey, California. Evelyn was the daughter of Charles Henry Marshall and the first wife of Marshall Field III, making Suarez the stepfather of Barbara Field, Bettine Field, and Marshall Field IV. His wife was also the sister-in-law of Brooke Astor.

After his death in 1974, Suarez was interred at Woodlawn Cemetery in The Bronx, New York. His legacy endures through his influential garden designs, particularly Villa Vizcaya, which remains a testament to his mastery of blending Renaissance and French baroque styles with innovative spatial planning.

title: Ivan Perišić
text:
Ivan Perišić is a highly versatile and decorated Croatian footballer, widely regarded as one of the greatest players in his country's history. Born on February 2, 1989, he is known for his ambidexterity and ability to play as a winger, wing-back, or even in attacking midfield roles. His professional career began in the youth academies of Hajduk Split and Sochaux, though he never made a first-team appearance for either club. After a brief loan spell at Belgian club Roeselare, he joined Club Brugge in 2009, where he quickly made a name for himself. In the 2010–11 season, he won the Belgian Pro League top goalscorer award and was named Belgian Footballer of the Year after scoring 22 league goals.

Perišić's success in Belgium caught the attention of Borussia Dortmund, who signed him in 2011 for around €5 million. He contributed to Dortmund's 2011–12 Bundesliga title but later faced reduced playing time under Jürgen Klopp, leading to a transfer to VfL Wolfsburg in 2013 for €8 million. At Wolfsburg, he became a key player, scoring 10 goals in the 2013–14 season and helping the team win the 2015 DFB-Pokal.

In 2015, Perišić moved to Inter Milan for €16 million, where he quickly established himself as a crucial player. Over five seasons, he scored 37 goals and provided 33 assists in all competitions, including a standout 2016–17 campaign with 11 goals and 10 assists. He won the 2020–21 Serie A title, the 2021 Supercoppa Italiana, and the 2021–22 Coppa Italia with Inter. His 2019 loan spell at Bayern Munich was particularly successful, as he won the treble—Bundesliga, DFB-Pokal, and Champions League—scoring in both the Champions League final and the semi-final thrashing of Barcelona.

Internationally, Perišić has been a key figure for Croatia since his debut in 2011. He has represented his country at multiple European Championships (2012, 2016, 2020, 2024) and World Cups (2014, 2018, 2022). His most memorable moment came in the 2018 World Cup final, where he scored an equalizer in extra time against France. Croatia eventually lost 4–2 but won a bronze medal in the 2022 World Cup. With 18 goal contributions in major tournaments, he holds the record for the most by a Croatian player.

Perišić's career has been marked by consistency, adaptability, and success at both club and international levels, cementing his legacy as one of Croatia's finest footballers. After leaving Bayern, he returned to Inter and later joined PSV in the Eredivisie, continuing to showcase his world-class abilities.

title: Daniel Alexander Cameron
text:
Daniel Alexander Cameron was a Canadian politician from Nova Scotia who played a notable role in the province’s early 20th-century politics. Born on December 10, 1870, in Sydney River, Nova Scotia, he was the son of John and Isabella (Macdonald) Cameron. He received his early education at Sydney Academy before attending Dalhousie University, where he earned a Bachelor of Laws degree. After being admitted to the bar in October 1893, he began practicing law in Sydney the following year. His legal career laid the foundation for his later political involvement.

Cameron’s political career began with local government roles. He served on the County Council from 1900 to 1911 and was the stipendiary magistrate for Sydney from 1905 to 1911. In 1911, he was appointed treasurer and solicitor for the Municipality of Cape Breton, a position that further solidified his public service credentials. His transition to provincial politics came in 1916 when he was elected to the Nova Scotia House of Assembly for the electoral district of Cape Breton as a member of the Liberal Party. However, his first term was short-lived, as he was defeated in the 1920 election.

From 1921 to 1923, Cameron served as a member of the Legislative Council of Nova Scotia, where he also held the position of Minister Without Portfolio in the cabinet of Premier George Henry Murray. He resigned from the Legislative Council in 1923 and successfully ran for the House of Assembly in the Victoria County electoral district. This election marked the beginning of his tenure as Provincial Secretary in the cabinet of Premier Ernest Howard Armstrong, a role he held from 1923 to 1925.

After resigning in 1930, Cameron attempted to enter federal politics, running as the Liberal candidate for the electoral district of Cape Breton South in the 1930 federal election. However, he was unsuccessful in this campaign. His political fortunes improved in 1935 when he was elected to the Nova Scotia House of Assembly for the electoral district of Cape Breton North and Victoria. He served in this capacity until his death in office on September 4, 1937, making him one of the first Nova Scotian legislators of the 20th century to die while holding office.

Cameron’s political career was marked by both local and provincial service, as well as a brief foray into federal politics. His roles in municipal government, the Legislative Council, and the provincial cabinet demonstrated his versatility and commitment to public service. Although his time in office was cut short by his death, he left a notable legacy as a prominent figure in Nova Scotia’s early 20th-century political landscape.

title: Muhammad Qutb
text:
Muhammad Ibrahim Husayn Shadhili Qutb, born on 26 April 1919 in the Egyptian village of Musha near Asyut, was an Islamic scholar and the younger brother of the influential revolutionary Sayyid Qutb. As the second oldest of five children, he moved to Helwan near Cairo after his father’s death in 1933. He pursued higher education, earning a degree in English literature from Cairo University in 1940 and later obtaining diplomas in psychology and education.

Qutb’s career was deeply intertwined with his brother’s political activism. In 1965, he was arrested alongside his brother, Sayyid, who was later executed in 1966 for alleged involvement in a plot to overthrow the Egyptian government. After Sayyid’s execution, Muhammad Qutb fled to Saudi Arabia, where he became a prominent figure in promoting his brother’s radical Islamic ideas. He worked as a professor of Islamic Studies, teaching at Umm al-Qura University in Mecca and King Abdulaziz University in Jeddah. Among his students were notable figures like Osama bin Laden and Ayman al-Zawahiri, both of whom were influenced by his teachings. Bin Laden frequently attended Qutb’s lectures and later recommended his book, *Concepts that Should be Corrected*, in a 2004 videotape.

In Saudi Arabia, Qutb played a key role in spreading his brother’s ideology, particularly by editing and publishing Sayyid Qutb’s works. He also worked to bridge ideological gaps between radical Islamists and more conservative Muslims, including members of the Muslim Brotherhood. While he initially supported the concept of *jahiliyya* (a state of pagan ignorance), he later distanced himself from extreme interpretations, publicly opposing *takfir* (declaring Muslims as unbelievers) and asserting that Saudi Arabia was not a *jahiliyya* state. He also sought to reconcile the Muslim Brotherhood’s doctrines with the dominant Salafist ideology in Saudi Arabia.

One of his most notable students was Safar al-Hawali, who defended his dissertation under Qutb’s supervision in 1986. Qutb was so impressed by al-Hawali’s work that he declared the student had surpassed him. Al-Hawali later became a leading figure in the *sahwa* (Islamist awakening) movement, which blended Wahhabism with Sayyid Qutb’s radical ideas.

Qutb’s writings were deeply critical of the modern Muslim world, which he believed had deviated from true Islamic teachings. He attributed the weakness of Muslim societies to both internal moral decay and external threats, particularly from Western powers, which he claimed were controlled by Jews. His anti-Semitic views were influenced by conspiracy theories like *The Protocols of the Elders of Zion*, and he argued that Western cultural imperialism was systematically undermining Islamic values. He particularly opposed the education of girls and the rise of feminism, which he saw as tools to corrupt Muslim society.

Qutb also defended Islamic slavery, including concubinage, arguing that it was more humane than Western practices. He claimed that Islam elevated slaves spiritually, contrasting this with what he described as the "animalistic" nature of Western sexuality.

Throughout his life, Qutb authored 36 books, including *Jahiliyya in the Twentieth Century* and *Islam: the Misunderstood Religion*, which expanded on his brother’s ideas. His works gained notoriety, with *Jahiliyya in the Twentieth Century* and Sayyid Qutb’s *Milestones* being labeled as terrorist handbooks by authorities. His teachings influenced the Sahwa movement and other Islamist groups, particularly in Saudi Arabia.

Muhammad Qutb died on 4 April 2014 in a hospital in Mecca at the age of 94. His legacy remains significant in Islamist thought, with his writings and lectures continuing to shape radical and conservative Islamic discourse.

title: Gemma Arterton
text:
Gemma Christina Arterton, born on 2 February 1986 in Gravesend, Kent, is a British actress with a diverse career in film, television, and theatre. She was born with polydactyly, a condition involving extra fingers, which was corrected shortly after birth. Her mother, Sally-Anne Heap, runs a cleaning business, while her father, Barry J. Arterton, is a welder. Her parents divorced when she was young, and she grew up on a council estate with her mother and younger sister, Hannah, who is also an actress. Arterton’s matrilineal great-grandmother was a German-Jewish concert violinist. She attended Gravesend Grammar School for Girls and later studied Performing Arts at North Kent College before graduating from the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in 2008.

Arterton’s professional acting career began while she was still at drama school, with a role in *Capturing Mary* (2007). Her stage debut came at the Globe Theatre in Shakespeare’s *Love’s Labour’s Lost*, where she played Rosaline. That same year, she made her film debut in *St Trinian’s* as Head Girl Kelly. In 2008, she gained international recognition as Bond Girl Strawberry Fields in *Quantum of Solace*, earning an Empire Award for Best Newcomer. That year, she also starred in the BBC adaptation of *Tess of the d'Urbervilles* and played Elizabeth Bennet in *Lost in Austen*.

One of her most challenging roles came in 2009’s *The Disappearance of Alice Creed*, where she played a kidnapped woman in a physically and emotionally demanding performance. She later appeared in major Hollywood films such as *Clash of the Titans* (2010), *Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time* (2010), and *Hansel & Gretel: Witch Hunters* (2013). In 2015, she starred in *Gemma Bovery*, a French-language adaptation of *Madame Bovary*, for which she learned French.

Arterton has also had a notable stage career, performing in *The Little Dog Laughed* (2010), *The Duchess of Malfi* (2014), *Made in Dagenham* (2014), *Nell Gwynn* (2016), and *Saint Joan* (2017). Her work in *Made in Dagenham* and *Nell Gwynn* earned her Olivier Award nominations, and she won an Evening Standard Theatre Award for the former.

In 2016, she founded Rebel Park Productions, a company focused on female-led projects. She produced and starred in *The Escape* (2017), which earned her critical acclaim and a Harper’s Bazaar Woman of the Year Award. She has also been involved in advocacy for gender equality, supporting movements like Time’s Up and ERA 50:50.

Her later film roles include *Their Finest* (2016), *Vita and Virginia* (2018), *Murder Mystery* (2019), and *The King’s Man* (2021), where she played Agent Galahad. She reprised the role in the upcoming sequel, *The Traitor King*.

Arterton has been married twice: first to Stefano Catelli (2010–2015) and later to actor Rory Keenan (from 2019). She and Keenan welcomed their first son in December 2022.

Throughout her career, Arterton has balanced commercial film roles with independent and theatrical work, demonstrating versatility across genres. She remains an active supporter of gender equality in the entertainment industry.

title: Jeremy Corbyn
text:
Jeremy Bernard Corbyn, born on 26 May 1949 in Chippenham, Wiltshire, is a British politician who has served as the Member of Parliament (MP) for Islington North since 1983. A lifelong member of the Labour Party until his expulsion in 2024, he was also a member of the Socialist Campaign Group and served as Leader of the Opposition and Labour Party leader from 2015 to 2020. Ideologically, Corbyn identifies as a socialist, positioning himself firmly on the political left.

Corbyn’s early life was shaped by his parents, who were Labour Party members and peace campaigners. After attending Castle House School and Adams Grammar School, he joined the Labour Party at 16 and became involved in the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) and anti-Vietnam War protests. He worked briefly as a reporter before spending two years in Jamaica as a youth worker and geography teacher. Upon returning to the UK, he became a trade union representative and later a councillor in Haringey. In 1983, he was elected as MP for Islington North, a seat he has held ever since.

Throughout his early career, Corbyn was known for his activist stances, including opposition to apartheid, support for the miners' strike, and involvement in the Anti-Apartheid Movement and Anti-Fascist Action. He was a vocal critic of the Iraq War and chaired the Stop the War Coalition from 2011 to 2015. His outspoken views often led him to vote against the Labour whip, even during New Labour governments.

In 2015, following Labour’s defeat in the general election, Corbyn was elected as Labour leader in a surprise victory. His leadership took the party significantly to the left, advocating policies such as renationalising public utilities, reducing military interventionism, and reversing austerity measures. Despite initially being critical of the European Union, he supported the Remain campaign in the 2016 Brexit referendum. His leadership was marked by both success and controversy. In the 2017 general election, Labour increased its vote share by 10 percentage points, the largest rise since 1945. However, his leadership also faced criticism over allegations of antisemitism within the party, which he denied were systemic but acknowledged required stronger disciplinary action.

The 2019 general election proved disastrous for Labour, with the party losing 60 seats and falling to 202 MPs, its lowest total since 1935. Corbyn announced his resignation as leader in 2020, though he remained in place until Keir Starmer’s election in April of that year. Controversy continued to follow him when he was suspended from the party after suggesting allegations of antisemitism had been exaggerated for political reasons. In 2024, after being barred from standing as a Labour candidate, he ran as an independent and won re-election in Islington North. Later that year, he and fellow independent MP Zarah Sultana announced the formation of a new political party.

Corbyn’s political career has been defined by his unwavering left-wing principles, grassroots activism, and controversial alliances, particularly with groups like Sinn Féin and the IRA during the Troubles. Despite his polarising reputation, his leadership significantly increased Labour’s membership and reshaped the party’s ideological direction. However, his tenure was also marked by internal strife, electoral setbacks, and ongoing debates about antisemitism within Labour.

title: Jackie Shroff
text:
Jackie Shroff, born Jaikishan Kakubhai Shroff on 1 February 1957 in Mumbai, is a veteran Indian actor and former model who has primarily worked in the Hindi film industry. Over his four-decade-long career, he has appeared in more than 250 films across 13 languages, earning several accolades, including four Filmfare Awards. His journey in Bollywood began with an uncredited role in *Swami Dada* (1982), but he gained fame with his lead debut in Subhash Ghai’s *Hero* (1983), which turned him into an overnight star. The film’s success marked the start of a prolific career, with Shroff delivering hits almost every year in the 1980s and 1990s. Some of his most notable films from this period include *Teri Meherbaniyan* (1985), *Karma* (1986), *Ram Lakhan* (1989), *Tridev* (1989), *Khalnayak* (1993), *Rangeela* (1995), *Border* (1997), and *Bandhan* (1998). His performance in *Parinda* (1989) earned him his first Filmfare Award for Best Actor, while *1942: A Love Story* (1994) and *Rangeela* (1995) won him consecutive Filmfare Awards for Best Supporting Actor.

In the 2000s, Shroff transitioned to more supporting and antagonist roles, appearing in films like *Refugee* (2000), *Mission Kashmir* (2000), *Devdas* (2002), and *Dhoom 3* (2013). He continued to showcase his versatility in roles across various languages, including Punjabi (*Sardar Saab*, 2017), Konkani (*Soul Curry*, 2017), Tamil (*Bigil*, 2019; *Jailer*, 2023), and Telugu (*Saaho*, 2019). His work in *Soul Curry* earned him the Goa State Award for Best Actor.

Beyond films, Shroff has been involved in television, hosting shows like *Lehrein*, *Chitrahaar*, and the investigative series *Missing*. He also judged *India’s Magic Star* and made appearances in digital series like *Criminal Justice* (2019). In his personal life, Shroff is an environmentalist who owns an organic farm. He married Ayesha Dutt, a model turned producer, in 1987, and they have two children: actor Tiger Shroff and entrepreneur Krishna Shroff. The couple co-founded Jackie Shroff Entertainment Limited and previously owned 10% shares in Sony TV.

Shroff is also known for his social activism, supporting causes such as HIV/AIDS awareness, female foeticide abolition, and Thalassemia treatment. He has funded education and medical care for underprivileged children and donated an ambulance to an animal shelter in memory of his late pet dog. Among his many awards, he received a Special Honour Jury Award for outstanding contribution to Indian cinema, the Raj Kapoor Special Contribution Award, and a Filmfare Short Film Award for Best Actor. He was also honored with a Doctor of Arts degree for his contributions to cinema.

title: Jeff Long (athletic director)
text:
Jeffrey Paul Long, born on September 21, 1959, is an American athletics administrator who has held notable positions at several universities. He most recently served as the athletic director at the University of Kansas before his departure in 2021. Long’s career in athletics administration has spanned multiple institutions, including the University of Arkansas, the University of Pittsburgh, the University of Oklahoma, the University of Michigan, Virginia Tech, and Eastern Kentucky University. His educational background includes a bachelor’s degree in economics from Ohio Wesleyan University (1982) and a master’s degree in education from Miami University (1983).

Long’s tenure at the University of Arkansas began in 2008, where he succeeded longtime athletic director Frank Broyles. Before Arkansas, he had briefly served as the athletic director at the University of Pittsburgh, taking over after Steve Pederson left for the University of Nebraska. One of his most controversial decisions at Arkansas was hiring Bobby Petrino as the football coach in 2008. However, in April 2012, Long fired Petrino after it was revealed that Petrino had been involved in an extramarital affair with Jessica Dorrell, a former Arkansas volleyball player whom Petrino had hired for a staff position in the football program. The scandal intensified when Petrino attempted to conceal the affair following a motorcycle accident in which Dorrell was a passenger. Long’s termination letter to Petrino emphasized that he would never have approved Dorrell’s hiring had he known about the relationship. The scandal also led to financial improprieties, as Petrino had secretly given Dorrell $20,000 as a Christmas gift, which could have exposed the university to legal risks. Petrino’s firing led to a tumultuous period for Arkansas football, with John L. Smith serving as interim coach in 2012 before Bret Bielema was hired the following year.

In 2013, Long was appointed as the first chairman of the College Football Playoff selection committee, a prestigious role that further cemented his influence in college sports. However, his time at Arkansas came to an abrupt end in November 2017, when the university announced his dismissal. The decision was attributed to a loss of support from fans, alumni, donors, and university leadership, though no specific reasons were publicly stated.

In 2018, Long became the athletic director at the University of Kansas, where he aimed to reverse the team’s prolonged struggles, as the Jayhawks had not had a winning football season since 2008. One of his first major moves was firing head coach David Beaty and replacing him with Les Miles, a longtime acquaintance from their days at the University of Michigan in the late 1980s. However, Miles’ tenure at Kansas was short-lived, as he was forced out in 2021 due to a sexual harassment scandal dating back to his time at LSU. At a press conference following Miles’ departure, Long expressed disappointment, stating that Miles had assured him there were no past issues that could harm the university. He claimed to have only learned of the allegations from media reports, despite being informed about a legal dispute in Louisiana earlier in the year. The following day, Long himself left Kansas, with university Chancellor Douglas Girod stating that the decision was made in the school’s best interest. Long later admitted that his departure was not entirely voluntary, confirming that he had been relieved of his duties but was allowed to resign publicly to maintain dignity.

Outside of his professional career, Long is married to Fanny Gellrich, and the couple has two daughters. His career has been marked by high-profile hires, controversies, and eventual departures from major athletics programs, reflecting both the challenges and pressures of leading college sports departments.

title: Sami Shalom Chetrit
text:
Sami Shalom Chetrit is a Moroccan-born Hebrew poet, interdisciplinary scholar, and Israeli social and peace activist. Born in Errachidia, Morocco, in 1960, he moved to Israel at the age of three and grew up in Ashdod. He earned his BA, MA, and PhD in political science from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, as well as an MA in International Affairs from Columbia University in New York. Currently, he resides in New York City, where he teaches Hebrew language, literature, and culture, as well as Middle Eastern studies at Queens College in Flushing.

Chetrit has been a prominent figure in Mizrahi activism, advocating for social justice and cultural freedom. He co-founded Kedma, an alternative school system that promoted equal opportunities and a multicultural curriculum, and was among the founders of the Mizrahi Democratic Rainbow Coalition, which campaigns for social justice and peace in Israel-Palestine. He identifies as an Arab Jew, reflecting his cultural and political identity.

Chetrit has authored numerous books, articles, and poems on Israeli society, politics, and culture. His notable works include *Intra-Jewish Conflict in Israel: White Jews, Black Jews* (2010), which explores ethnic tensions within Israeli society, and *The Mizrahi Struggle in Israel: Between Oppression and Liberation, Identification and Alternative, 1948–2003* (2004, 2005), which examines the historical and political struggles of Mizrahi Jews in Israel. He has also contributed to academic journals and edited volumes, discussing issues such as Mizrahi politics, education, and the relationship between Ashkenazi and Mizrahi Jews. His literary contributions include four poetry collections, a novel, and translations of his work into multiple languages. Notable collections include *Poems in Ashdodian* (2003), *Jews* (2008), and *A Mural With No Wall: Kasida to Mahmud Darwish* (2008), which reflects his engagement with Arab and Jewish cultural traditions.

In addition to his written work, Chetrit has produced two documentary films. *The Black Panthers (in Israel) Speak* (2003) documents the social-protest movement of the 1970s, while *Az’i Ayima (Come Mother)* (2009) focuses on Moroccan immigrant women in Israel. Both films have been screened at international festivals, including the African Diaspora Film Festival in New York and the DocAviv International Film Festival in Tel Aviv.

Chetrit’s work spans multiple disciplines, blending poetry, academia, and activism to address issues of identity, social justice, and cultural representation. His contributions have been recognized in both Hebrew and English-speaking academic and literary circles, making him a significant voice in discussions about Mizrahi identity, Israeli society, and the broader Middle East.

title: Shin Jea-hwan
text:
Shin Jea-hwan is a South Korean artistic gymnast born on March 3, 1998, in Seoul. He is best known for winning the gold medal in the men's vault event at the 2020 Summer Olympics in Tokyo, making him the second South Korean gymnast to achieve this feat after Yang Hak-seon's victory in 2012. Shin also holds the distinction of being a two-time World Cup champion on vault, triumphing at the 2020 Melbourne and 2020 Baku events.

Shin's early career began to take shape when he made his senior international debut at the 2019 Zhaoqing World Cup, where he secured a silver medal on vault and finished fourth on floor. He continued to compete on the 2020 World Cup circuit, focusing on both vault and floor, and claimed two gold medals on vault. His consistent performances led him to the top of the qualification series for the 2020 Olympics, though the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted the series. The International Gymnastics Federation (FIG) later decided to hold a final qualifying event, the 2021 Doha World Cup, to finalize Olympic spots. Despite finishing fifth in Doha, Shin maintained his series lead over Japan's Hidenobu Yonekura due to a tiebreaker, securing his Olympic qualification.

At the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, Shin qualified for the vault final in first place, tying with Armenia's Artur Davtyan with a score of 14.866. The tiebreaker was decided in his favor because of his higher individual vault score (15.100 compared to Davtyan's 15.000). In the final, he faced another tiebreaker scenario against Denis Ablyazin of the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC), with both men scoring 14.783. Once again, Shin's higher individual vault score (14.833 versus 14.800) gave him the advantage, securing his Olympic gold medal.

Shin attended the Korea National Sport University and graduated in 2020. He relocated to Jecheon in 2021 and has expressed admiration for his teammate and fellow Olympic champion, Yang Hak-seon. His success in vault has cemented his reputation as one of South Korea's top gymnasts, continuing the country's strong tradition in the event. Shin's Olympic victory was particularly notable as it marked the second time a South Korean gymnast had won gold in the men's vault, following Yang's historic win in 2012. His performances on the international stage have solidified his place among the world's elite gymnasts.

title: Nuh Omar
text:
Nuh Omar, born on June 5, 1988, is a director and screenwriter who hails from Karachi, Pakistan. He comes from a prominent family, being the grandson of entrepreneur Safdar Kureishi and the older brother of Omar Kureishi. His family also includes notable figures like Hanif Kureishi and Maki Kureishi. Nuh attended Karachi Grammar School, where he was a classmate of Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, and has an older sister and a younger brother. His mother, Pakistan’s first female sports photojournalist, played a significant role in shaping his early life.

After completing his early education, Nuh pursued film studies at the New York Film Academy in 2006, where he was part of its inaugural 2nd Year Film Program. He later earned a bachelor’s degree in the Science of Film from Full Sail University. Following his education, he interned under Scott Gardenhour at The Institute and worked as a freelance assistant director, contributing to several award-winning short films. He also worked as a documentarian. In 2011, his short film *We're Americans, Eh?* won both the Audience Award and Best Wardrobe at the 24 Hour Film Festival.

In 2012, Nuh returned to Pakistan and collaborated with Y Productions and producer Ayesha Jalil to direct a series of short films for Engro Corporation’s Excellence Awards. One of these films, *Mojiza-e-Fun (The Miracle of Art)*, featured sculptor Shahid Sajjad in what would be the artist’s final project before his death. Around the same time, he engaged in freelance writing and directing for online projects and ghostwrote commercials. He later joined DeVida Lifestyle, an entertainment channel, as an in-house and promo director before leaving in mid-2012.

Early in 2013, Nuh was hired by the advertising agency IAL Saatchi & Saatchi, where he worked on global Procter & Gamble brands such as Head & Shoulders, Safeguard, Pampers, and Commander Safeguard under COO Imtisal Abbasi and ECD Rashna Abdi. He left the company in early 2014 to return to filmmaking.

In November 2015, Nuh began directing and writing episodes for *The Fortress of Dorkness*, a YouTube channel dedicated to pop culture movies and comics, created by producer Christian Villarreal. By 2018, the channel had produced over 100 episodes, all written and directed by Nuh, before going on hiatus in 2019 with plans for future content.

In 2019, Nuh collaborated with writer Mark Davis to develop *The Alexandrian* (originally titled *Cleopatra*), an episodic historical drama exploring the dynasty of Cleopatra. Additionally, he has been working on *The Porter & The Stone*, a modern adaptation of Oscar Wilde’s *The Happy Prince*, which has earned multiple awards, including Best Short at Screencraft’s Public Domain Competition in 2021 and finalist status at the Atlanta Film Festival Screenplay Competition in 2022. By early 2022, the screenplay was ranked number one in both the Family and Family-Short categories on Coverfly, placing it in the top 1% of all projects.

Another notable project is *A Matter of Time*, a TV pilot screenplay co-written with Christian Villarreal, which won the grand prize at Filmmatic’s TV Pilot Awards Season 6 as Best TV Pilot. The project is currently being shopped for production. Nuh is also developing *I'm Here*, a TV series based on his own experiences in the American heartland, seen through the perspective of a tabloid journalist interviewing cryptids and folklore creatures. Initially conceived in 2007, the project was briefly adapted into a comic book before returning to its television roots.

Currently, Nuh is working with production company Rustic Lightbulb and producer Severn Lang on *The Universe at Midnight* and the feature film *Tijuana Bible*, both of which he will write and direct. *The Universe at Midnight* is expected to begin production in 2022. Additionally, he is writing two feature films: *The Imaginary Friend Society*, a family-oriented story about imaginary friends, and *Ophelia*, a tale about a man chosen to become the next form of death and his relationship with a Djinn named Ophelia.

Nuh Omar splits his time between Karachi, Pakistan, and Los Angeles, California. He has been open about his struggles with depression and advocates for mental health awareness. His work spans film, television, and advertising, showcasing his versatility and creativity in storytelling.

title: José Hernández Delgadillo
text:
José Hernández Delgadillo (1927–2000) was a Mexican painter and muralist who carried forward the traditions of Mexican muralism in the late 20th century, though his politically charged work often made him controversial. Born in Tepeapulco, Hidalgo, to a poor rural family, he spent his early years working on farms, in construction, and as a furniture maker before moving to Mexico City in 1945. There, he studied painting and architectural drawing under Antonio Navarrete Tejero, supporting himself by painting portraits. After his first solo exhibition in 1954, he pursued advanced training at the Escuela Nacional de Pintura, Escultura y Grabado "La Esmeralda" (1955–1960), where he encountered Pablo O’Higgins, a key figure in Mexican muralism, which deepened his commitment to the movement’s social and political ideals.

Hernández Delgadillo’s career spanned painting, sculpture, and murals, with his most enduring contributions being his over 160 murals in Mexico and the United States. His early works, such as *Hombres* (1961), earned him recognition at international biennials and a French government grant, allowing him to exhibit in Europe. However, his later work—particularly after the 1968 student uprising—became increasingly political, aligning with the struggles of laborers, students, and marginalized communities. Many of his murals, created in collaboration with students and activist groups, were executed in a day, often accompanied by performances and discussions. His most prominent works include murals at universities, technical schools, and public spaces, such as the Centro Residencial Morelos in Mexico City, where his critical monument nearly jeopardized his career. His first U.S. mural, in San Fernando, California (1981), was commissioned by a Chicano organization, and he later created works in California’s agricultural and Latino communities.

Politically active, Hernández Delgadillo wrote a weekly column for *Excélsior* (1980–1983), ran for office with the Partido Mexicano de Trabajadores (1985), and was a pre-candidate for president with the PRD (1987). Though he supported Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas’s campaign, creating murals for it, his radical views often placed him at odds with mainstream institutions.
