His artistry blended expressionism with monumental, primal figures, often denouncing violence and social injustice. Critics noted his synthesis of classicism and personal expression, with his work evoking indigenous heritage and exploitation. Despite his contributions, many of his murals have deteriorated or been destroyed due to their controversial messages, leading to efforts in the 2010s to restore and preserve them, particularly in Pachuca.

His legacy includes membership in the Salón de la Plástica Mexicana, the establishment of an annual muralism competition (1997), and a posthumous retrospective (2009). However, his obscurity stems from his unpopular political stance, with the first biography, *Muros de Insomnio* (2008), published only after his death. His wife, Beatriz Zamora, and their three children survived him. Today, his work is recognized for its unwavering commitment to social justice, though it remains underappreciated outside activist circles.

title: Antonio Leviste
text:
Antonio Leviste, born on January 16, 1940, is a prominent Filipino politician and businessman who served as Governor of Batangas from 1972 to 1980. Coming from a well-established Batangueño family known for its influence in business and politics, Leviste has had a multifaceted career spanning government service, environmental advocacy, and real estate. He was married to Senator Loren Legarda but separated from her before the 2004 election campaign. His daughter from a previous marriage, Toni Leviste, is a decorated equestrian athlete who has competed in the Asian Games.

Leviste's political career began after graduating from the Lyceum of the Philippines in 1959, where he later became president of the Student Varsitarian, a prestigious student organization. During his tenure as governor, he held several key positions, including chairmanship of the Regional Development Council and the Program for Forest Ecosystem Management, as well as vice presidency of the League of Governors and City Mayors. His environmental initiatives, particularly in forest ecosystem management, earned him the "Ten Outstanding Young Men of the Philippines" (TOYM) award in Public Administration. His programs in reforestation continue to be regarded as models in environmental conservation.

Beyond politics, Leviste has been deeply involved in business and real estate. He was recognized as the "Realtor of the Year" by the Business Writers Association of the Philippines and served as a director in several government agencies, including the People's Homesite and Housing Corporation (now the National Housing Authority), the Philippine Ports Authority, the Philippine Aerospace Development Corporation, and the Philippine Tourism Authority. He co-founded the Pasay Board of Realtors and the Philippine Association of Real Estate Boards, and later became chairman of the Philippine Leisure and Retirement Authority (now the Philippine Retirement Authority). Additionally, he holds the rank of Lieutenant Commander in the Philippine Navy Reserve Force and serves as the Honorary Consul General of the State of Palestine. Currently, he leads the Leviste Group of Companies, a real estate firm specializing in housing, subdivisions, condominiums, and resort development. He is also the charter president of the Resort Association of the Philippines and a co-founder of the Tourism Council of the Philippines.

Leviste's career took a controversial turn in 2009 when he was convicted of homicide in the killing of his longtime aide, Rafael de las Alas. Although Leviste claimed self-defense, the Makati Regional Trial Court sentenced him to six to twelve years in prison. He served his sentence at the National Bilibid Prison in Muntinlupa and was released on December 6, 2013, after being granted parole. Despite his legal troubles, Leviste has remained an influential figure in both business and public life.

title: Sandra Pisani
text:
Sandra Pisani was an Australian field hockey player and coach born on 23 January 1959 in Adelaide, South Australia, where she spent most of her life. She died on 19 April 2022 after a battle with cancer. Pisani had a distinguished career in hockey, both as a player and in administrative roles, contributing significantly to the sport's development in Australia. She played 85 international matches for Australia, debuting in 1981 at the World Cup in Buenos Aires. She served as the national team captain from 1985 to 1987, leading Australia in several major tournaments, including the 1986 World Cup and the 1987 Champions Trophy, where the team won a silver medal. Her most notable achievement as a player came at the 1988 Summer Olympics in Seoul, where she was part of the Australian team that won the nation’s first-ever Olympic gold medal in field hockey.

At the club level, Pisani began her career in 1976 with the Burnside Hockey Club, playing in A grade and winning eight premierships over 15 years. She was awarded the club’s Best and Fairest in 1985 and 1987 and later received Life Membership in 2002. She also won the Association Medal for South Australia’s Best and Fairest Player in 1985 and 1992. In 1991, she moved to Port Adelaide, where she played and coached the team from 1991 to 1994. Under her leadership, the team improved significantly, winning a premiership in 1993 and earning her the Hockey SA Coach of the Year award. She later coached the Woodville Hockey Club and in 2012, she shared the Hockey SA Coach of the Year award with Rachel Hampton.

Pisani was highly involved in state-level hockey, playing for South Australia in the Australian Hockey League for the Southern Suns from 1978 to 1992, including five years as the team’s captain. She later took on mentoring, coaching, and managerial roles with the team. Her contributions to the sport were recognized with her inclusion on the South Australian Sports Institute Hockey Honour Roll in 1988, following her Olympic gold medal win. In 1989, she was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia (OAM) for her service to hockey. She also served on the board of Hockey SA and was a delegate for the Australian Women’s Hockey Association. In 2000, she received the Australian Sports Medal for her role in the 1988 Olympic team and her work as a selector. In 2003, she was part of the 1988 Olympic team that received the Team Sport Australia Award at the Sport Australia Hall of Fame Awards, recognizing their historic gold medal victory. She was inducted into the South Australian Sport Hall of Fame in 2015 and was twice a finalist in the Caltex SA Sports Star of the Year Award.

Beyond her playing career, Pisani made significant contributions to Australian hockey as a selector and administrator. From 1993 to 2000, she served as the National Women’s Senior Selector for the Hockeyroos, including as the Head Selector during the team’s golden era, when they won consecutive Olympic gold medals at the 1996 and 2000 Summer Games under coach Ric Charlesworth. She later became a National Youth Selector and in 2014, she served as Team Manager for the Women’s Australia A development tour to China and Japan. Throughout her career, Pisani demonstrated a deep commitment to the development of hockey in Australia, leaving a lasting legacy in the sport.

title: Paul Anka
text:
Paul Albert Anka, born on July 30, 1941, in Ottawa, Ontario, is a Canadian-American singer, songwriter, and actor with a prolific career spanning over six decades. His parents, Camelia Tannis and Andrew Emile "Andy" Anka Sr., were Lebanese Christian immigrants, with his father from Damascus, Syria, and his mother from Lebanon. Anka’s musical talent was nurtured early, as he sang in the St. Elias Antiochian Orthodox Cathedral choir and performed with a vocal trio called the Bobby Soxers in high school. His first single, "I Confess," was recorded at just 14 years old, but it was his 1957 hit "Diana" that catapulted him to fame, topping charts in Canada and the U.S. and becoming one of the best-selling singles by a Canadian artist. The song was inspired by a girl from his church, though he initially claimed it was for a former babysitter.

Anka’s early success continued with multiple Top 20 hits in 1958, including "It's Time to Cry" and "(All of a Sudden) My Heart Sings," establishing him as a leading teen idol. He toured with Buddy Holly and wrote "It Doesn't Matter Anymore," a song Holly recorded shortly before his death in 1959. Anka also composed the theme for *The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson* and wrote "Teddy" for Connie Francis. One of his most enduring contributions is the English lyrics for "My Way," originally a French song, which became Frank Sinatra’s signature tune. In the 1960s, Anka expanded into acting, appearing in films like *The Longest Day* (1962), where he also wrote the theme song, and *Girls Town* (1959). He became one of the first pop singers to perform in Las Vegas.

After over a decade without a major hit, Anka reinvented himself in the 1970s, teaming up with Odia Coates for the No. 1 hit "(You're) Having My Baby" (1974), followed by several Top 20 duets. He also recorded a popular jingle for Kodak, which he later adapted into the hit "Times of Your Life" (1976). His last Top 40 U.S. hit, "Hold Me 'Til the Mornin' Comes" (1983), featured backing vocals from Peter Cetera of Chicago. In the 1990s, he made a comeback with *A Body of Work* (1998), featuring collaborations with Celine Dion and Kenny G, and *Rock Swings* (2005), a big-band reimagining of rock songs.

Anka also collaborated with Michael Jackson, co-writing three songs, including "This Is It" and "Love Never Felt So Good," which became posthumous hits for Jackson. He had significant success internationally, particularly in Italy, where his 1962 hit "Ogni giorno" topped the charts, and in Finland, where he performed multiple times. He also ventured into acting in films like *3000 Miles to Graceland* (2001) and appeared in TV shows like *That '70s Show* and *Gilmore Girls*, where a character named her dog after him.

In his personal life, Anka was married three times, first to Anne de Zogheb (1963–2001), a model of Lebanese and English descent, with whom he had five children. He later married Swedish personal trainer Anna Åberg (2008–2010) and Lisa Pemberton (2016–2020). He became a U.S. citizen in 1990. Anka received numerous honors, including being named an Officer of the Order of Canada in 2004, and a street in Ottawa was named after him in 1972. His autobiography, *My Way*, was published in 2013.

Beyond music, Anka ventured into technology, co-founding ARHT Media, a holographic tech startup, in 2012. His career has left an indelible mark on pop culture, from his songwriting to his acting and business endeavors, solidifying his legacy as a multifaceted entertainer.

title: Chi Pu
text:
Chi Pu, born Nguyễn Thùy Chi on June 14, 1993, in Hanoi, Vietnam, is a prominent Vietnamese actress and singer. Her stage name, Chi Pu, is widely recognized in the entertainment industry. She first gained attention after placing in the Top 20 of Miss Teen Vietnam 2009, which opened doors for her to become a teen idol. By November 2016, she had amassed the highest number of followers among Vietnamese actresses on social media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube. Her early success set the stage for a diverse and prolific career in acting, singing, and digital content creation.

Chi Pu launched her acting career in 2013 with leading roles in the television dramas *Waterdrop* and *Happy Dream*, both broadcast on Vietnam National Television. That same year, she joined the popular television series *5S Online* and produced her first short film, *Under One Sky*, which earned a Golden Kite Award in 2014. She also starred in her first full-length film, *Thần tượng (The Talent)*, which won six Golden Kite Awards. Her horror movies *Chung cư ma (Hush)* and *Hương Ga (Rise)* gained critical acclaim, with the latter winning Best Vietnamese Film at the 2016 San Francisco International New Concept Film Festival.

In 2014, she starred in the high-rating television drama *Vẫn có em bên đời (You’re Always by My Side)*, earning her an HTV Award for Most Favorite Television Drama Actress. She also produced and starred in the short film *My Sunshine*, which received praise for its support of the LGBT community. The following year, she took a leading role in *Yêu (Love)*, an LGBT-themed film that grossed over half a million USD in its first three days and won the Golden Apricot Blossom Award for Best Movie. Chi Pu received nominations for Best Actress at the 2015 Golden Apricot Blossom Awards and Green Star Awards.

Beyond film, Chi Pu has hosted major shows like *Dancing with the Stars Kids Vietnam - Season 2* (2015) and *The Voice Kids Vietnam - Season 4* (2016). She also voiced the character Glim in the French animated film *Mune: Guardian of the Moon* and participated in the musical *Thiên đài (The Rooftop)*, an adaptation of a Chinese musical by Jay Chou. In 2016, she produced her first web series, *Wake Up*, which she also wrote, starred in, and composed the original soundtrack for. The series was funded by Chi Pu and brand sponsorships. She performed at international events like Viral Fest Asia 2016 in Indonesia and attended the Asia Artist Awards in Seoul, Korea.

Chi Pu officially began her singing career in 2017, gaining immediate attention. In 2023, she competed in the fourth season of the Chinese reality show *Sisters Who Make Waves*, where she placed sixth overall and won two sub-categories: "Fan Favorite" for her performance of *Shut Up and Dance* and "Overcoming Challenges." This earned her a spot in the 11-member girl group set to debut in the Chinese entertainment industry.

Beyond entertainment, Chi Pu is known for her fashion collaborations, being the first Vietnamese actress to launch her own fashion collections with TheBlueTshirt and PUSW. She has endorsed major brands like Yamaha Janus, Dove Vietnam, and OPPO Cameraphone. She was also the first Vietnamese artist to collaborate with Google for an advertising campaign. Known for her activism, Chi Pu has supported causes like disaster relief for flood victims in Central Vietnam, funding heart surgeries for children, and advocating against dog theft and rhino horn consumption as an ambassador for the "Come home Golden" campaign.

Her discography includes numerous singles, such as *Fighting Fighting* (from *Wake Up*), *Stay With Me* (from *LOVE*), and collaborations like *Tada X’mas* with Gil Lê. She has released music annually since 2017, covering various genres and themes.

Chi Pu’s achievements include Forbes Asia's Top 100 Digital Star (2020), TikTok Awards 2020 (Public Figure of the Year), and multiple acting and fashion accolades, including the ELLE Style Awards and Golden Kite Awards. Her multifaceted career as an actress, singer, producer, and activist has cemented her as one of Vietnam’s most influential digital stars.

title: Felipe (footballer, born 1977)
text:
Felipe Jorge Loureiro, commonly known as Felipe, is a Brazilian former footballer and current technical director of Vasco da Gama. Born on 2 September 1977 in Rio de Janeiro, he began his football journey at a young age, joining Vasco da Gama at just six years old for their futsal team. He transitioned to the field in 1990 at the age of 12 and made his professional debut for Vasco on 3 November 1996 in a 2–1 victory over Botafogo. Felipe quickly established himself as a key player, known for his left-footed playmaking style, earning the nickname "Maestro" due to his exceptional ball control, dribbling skills, and vision in orchestrating offensive plays. He scored his first senior goal on 30 August 1997 in a 3–2 win over Sport Recife and became a regular starter, contributing to Vasco's successful period during that time.

In May 1999, Felipe was sold to Italian club Roma for a reported $20 million, but the deal faced complications when manager Fabio Capello refused to accept him. The transfer was eventually canceled, and Felipe returned to Vasco, with Roma compensating the club with $2 million in 2002. In 2001, after a period of injury and disputes with Vasco's board over perceived underpayment, Felipe was loaned to Palmeiras but was released just a few months later. He then moved on loan to Atlético Mineiro before returning to Vasco in 2002, where he regained his starting position.

In 2002, Felipe ventured abroad, joining Turkish club Galatasaray, but his time there was short-lived as he left after featuring sparingly. He then signed with Flamengo in January 2003, where he became a key player in the 2004 campaign, often deployed as a right winger. Despite helping Flamengo win the 2004 Campeonato Carioca, the club narrowly avoided relegation in the same year. In January 2005, Felipe joined Fluminense, but his tenure was marred by injuries and disciplinary issues, including a 120-day suspension for assaulting an opponent during a Copa do Brasil match. His contract was terminated in October 2005 after further disagreements with the club.

Felipe then moved to Qatar, joining Al Sadd in November 2005. Over the next five seasons, he won multiple titles, including the Qatar Stars League, Emir of Qatar Cup, Qatar Cup, and Sheikh Jassim Cup, as well as earning individual accolades. In June 2010, he returned to Vasco, where he played until December 2012, when his contract was rescinded following disagreements with club officials. He briefly returned to Fluminense in January 2013 but left at the end of the year. After three months without a club, Felipe announced his retirement in March 2014 at the age of 36.

Felipe's international career included six appearances for the Brazilian national team, making his debut in a friendly against Yugoslavia in September 1998. He was part of Brazil's squad for the 2004 Copa América, which they won. His club career was marked by significant achievements, including winning the Campeonato Brasileiro Série A twice with Vasco, the Copa Libertadores in 1998, and multiple domestic and international titles with other clubs. He also received individual honors, such as being named the Copa do Brasil Player of the Year and being included in the South American Team of the Year in 1998.

After retiring, Felipe transitioned into coaching, first leading Tigres do Brasil in 2016 before resigning a few months later. He later worked as a football coordinator at Ponte Preta and Bangu, and briefly managed Confiança in 2022. In June 2024, he returned to Vasco as technical director, also serving as interim head coach on two occasions in 2024 and 2025. Felipe's career spanned both playing and coaching, marked by his technical ability, leadership, and contributions to Brazilian and international football.

title: Neil Sinclair
text:
Neil Sinclair, born on 23 February 1974 in Northern Ireland, was a professional boxer who competed between 1995 and 2010. During his career, he achieved notable success both at the amateur and professional levels. Before turning professional, Sinclair represented Ireland and Northern Ireland in amateur competitions. In 1992, he won a bronze medal at the Junior World Championships in Montreal while boxing for Ireland. Two years later, he secured a gold medal at the 1994 Commonwealth Games in Victoria, British Columbia, representing Northern Ireland.

Sinclair made his professional debut in April 1995 at the Ulster Hall in Belfast, defeating Marty Duke by knockout. This fight was part of a card that also featured Darren Corbett and marked the final professional bout of Damien Denny’s career. His early professional career set the stage for a journey that included regional titles and high-level challenges.

At the regional level, Sinclair captured the British welterweight title in 2001, a belt he held until 2003. He also contested the EBU European Union title in 2008, though the outcome of that fight is not detailed in the article. One of his most significant professional achievements came in May 2009 when he won the Irish light-middleweight title after stopping Henry Coyle at the Odyssey Arena in Belfast.

In June 2007, Sinclair briefly announced his retirement from boxing, but he soon reconsidered and returned to the sport within a few months. His professional career culminated in a world title challenge in 2010, when he fought for the WBO welterweight championship. However, the article does not specify the result of this bout.

Sinclair’s boxing record, which is referenced but not fully detailed in the article, can be found on external sites like BoxRec. His contributions to the sport are also noted in the "List of British welterweight boxing champions" due to his regional title victories. Additionally, his amateur achievements are recognized by the Commonwealth Games Federation, where his 1994 gold medal is documented.

Throughout his career, Sinclair demonstrated resilience and determination, from his early amateur successes to his professional pursuits, including a brief retirement and a return to the ring. His career spanned both international and regional competitions, showcasing his versatility and commitment to boxing. title: Peter Gallagher
text:
Peter Gallagher is an American actor born on August 19, 1955, in New York City. His parents were Mary Ann O'Shea, a bacteriologist, and Thomas Francis Gallagher Jr., an advertising executive. Raised in Armonk, New York, Gallagher was the youngest of three children and comes from an Irish Catholic background. He graduated from Tufts University, where he was involved in theater, performing in productions like *Stephen Sondheim's Company* and singing with the all-male a cappella group the Beelzebubs. After college, he studied acting at the William Esper Studio and with Mira Rostova.

Gallagher began his professional acting career in the early 1980s and gained early recognition for his role in *sex, lies, and videotape* (1989), directed by Steven Soderbergh. His film career includes notable roles in *Bob Roberts* (1992), *The Player* (1992), *Short Cuts* (1993), *While You Were Sleeping* (1995), *American Beauty* (1999), *Mr. Deeds* (2002), and *Palm Springs* (2020). On stage, he is best known for his performance as Sky Masterson in the 1992 Broadway revival of *Guys and Dolls*.

Television has been a significant part of Gallagher’s career, particularly for his role as Sandy Cohen, a public defender and lawyer, in the Fox series *The O.C.* (2003–2007). He also had recurring roles in *Law & Order: Special Victims Unit* as Deputy Chief William Dodds, *Californication* as Stacey Koons, *Grace & Frankie* as Nick, and *Covert Affairs* as Director of Clandestine Services Arthur Campbell. In *Zoey’s Extraordinary Playlist* (2020–2021), he portrayed Mitch Clarke, a character with progressive supranuclear palsy, and later appeared in *Grey’s Anatomy* (2021).

Gallagher has also ventured into music, releasing an album titled *7 Days in Memphis* in 2005. The album included a recording of "Don't Give Up On Me," which was featured in *The O.C.*, and a music video for "Still I Long For Your Kiss," in which he starred alongside his *The O.C.* co-star Kelly Rowan.

Gallagher has received several honors, including the P.T. Barnum Award and the "Light on the Hill" award from Tufts University in recognition of his contributions to media and entertainment. In 2015, he starred in the Broadway production of *On the Twentieth Century*, though he missed some performances due to illness. In 2024, he is set to return to Broadway in a play based on the life of Delia Ephron, titled *Left on Tenth*.

In his personal life, Gallagher is married to Paula Harwood and has two children, James and Kathryn. His daughter Kathryn is an actress and singer. Gallagher’s career has spanned film, television, theater, and music, making him a versatile and enduring figure in the entertainment industry.

title: Dascha Polanco
text:
Dascha Yolaine Polanco, born on December 3, 1982, in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, is an actress known for her roles in television and film. She moved to the United States as a child and was raised in Sunset Park, Brooklyn, and Miami by her father, a mechanic, and her mother, a cosmetologist. As the oldest of three siblings, she grew up with a brother and a sister. From an early age, Polanco dreamed of becoming an actress but struggled with self-doubt due to her weight, leading her to pursue a more traditional career path. She earned a bachelor’s degree in psychology from Hunter College, becoming the first in her family to attend college. After graduation, she worked in the healthcare industry, aiming to become a nurse, and held a position in hospital administration at Montefiore Medical Center in the Bronx while studying nursing. Despite her initial hesitation, she eventually decided to pursue acting, enrolling at BIH Studios in New York. It was during this time that she was signed by the talent agency Shirley Grant Management, marking the beginning of her acting career.

Polanco’s early roles included minor appearances in the television series *Unforgettable* and *NYC 22*. Her breakthrough came in 2012 when she was cast as Dayanara "Daya" Diaz in the Netflix series *Orange Is the New Black*. The role, which she played for several seasons, brought her significant recognition. In 2013, she appeared in the independent film *Gimme Shelter* and continued her work on *Orange Is the New Black* for its second season. In 2014, she was promoted from a recurring role to a series regular for the show’s third season, which premiered in 2015. During this period, she also appeared in the comedy films *The Cobbler* and *Joy* and starred in *The Perfect Match*.

In 2018, Polanco took on a recurring role in *The Assassination of Gianni Versace: American Crime Story*, and in 2019, she had recurring roles in the Netflix series *Russian Doll* and *When They See Us*. One of her most notable film roles came in 2021 when she played Cuca, one of the lead salon ladies, in the musical film *In the Heights*. Around the same time, she voiced Ms. Camilla Torres, the mother of Winston, in the animated series *Karma’s World*, which aired from 2021 to 2022. In 2025, she starred as Michelle Borgas in the Lifetime film *Terror Comes Knocking: The Marcela Borgas Story*, part of the network’s "Ripped from the Headlines" series.

Polanco’s personal life includes being a mother to two children, a daughter and a son. Notably, her daughter played a younger version of Polanco’s character in the fifth season of *Orange Is the New Black*, adding a personal touch to her career. Polanco’s journey from a hesitant aspiring actress to a recognized performer reflects her determination and resilience in the entertainment industry.

title: Joseph Kony
text:
Joseph Kony, born in September 1961 in Odek, Uganda, is an Acholi warlord and the founder of the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA), a militant group designated as a terrorist organization by the United Nations, European Union, and several governments, including the United States and the United Kingdom. Kony’s early life was marked by a brief education as an altar boy, but he dropped out at age 15. His family background was modest, with his father working as a farmer and lay catechist, while his mother was an Anglican farmer. Kony married Selly, with whom he had a son named Ali Ssalongo Kony. His childhood was reportedly marked by a quick temper and a tendency toward violence.

Kony’s rise to prominence began in 1987 when he founded the LRA, following his involvement in the Holy Spirit Movement, an earlier insurgency group. The LRA’s stated goal was to create a Christian state based on dominion theology, though its actions were characterized by extreme brutality. The group gained notoriety for abducting children, forcing them into roles as child soldiers and sex slaves. Over 66,000 children were estimated to have been abducted, and approximately 2 million people were internally displaced between 1986 and 2009. The LRA’s insurgency led to widespread atrocities, including mass killings, rape, and the destruction of villages.

In response to these crimes, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued arrest warrants for Kony and four other LRA leaders in 2005, charging them with war crimes and crimes against humanity. Kony remains at large, despite efforts by the Ugandan military, the United States, and the African Union to capture him. An Interpol Red Notice was issued for his arrest in 2006, and the U.S. designated him as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist in 2008.

The LRA’s insurgency was fueled by a mix of mysticism, Acholi nationalism, and a twisted interpretation of Christianity. Kony claimed to be a spiritual medium, asserting that he was guided by 13 spirits, including a Chinese one. He promoted polygamy, reportedly having 60 wives and fathering 42 children. His followers believed he possessed supernatural powers, using oil to protect them from bullets. The LRA’s ideology justified violence, including the killing of perceived enemies, under the guise of religious purification.

Kony’s forces clashed with Ugandan government troops and other regional militaries for decades. In 2008, the Ugandan army launched Operation Lightning Thunder in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in an attempt to capture him, but the operation failed. By 2017, the LRA’s strength had dwindled to around 100 fighters, prompting both the U.S. and Uganda to scale back their efforts to capture Kony. Despite this, he remained a fugitive as of 2024, with reports suggesting he was hiding in the Darfur region of Sudan or the Central African Republic (CAR).

Efforts to bring Kony to justice included the 2012 "Kony 2012" campaign, a viral documentary aimed at raising international awareness. However, the campaign was criticized for oversimplifying the conflict. In 2022, the ICC scheduled an in absentia hearing for Kony, the first of its kind, though he remained unapprehended. Meanwhile, former LRA commander Dominic Ongwen, who had been abducted as a child and rose through the ranks, surrendered in 2015 and was later convicted by the ICC in 2021 for crimes against humanity and war crimes.

Kony’s health has been a subject of speculation, with reports in 2013 suggesting he was in poor condition. His forces have been increasingly weakened, with former members defecting due to low morale. In April 2024, it was reported that 14 LRA fighters surrendered, leading to an attack on Kony’s camp by the Wagner Group, a Russian private military company, prompting him to flee toward Sudan.

Despite decades of conflict, Kony’s whereabouts remain uncertain, and he continues to evade justice. The LRA’s legacy of violence and the abduction of thousands of children have left deep scars on northern Uganda and neighboring regions, making Kony one of Africa’s most notorious war criminals.

title: Chris John (boxer)
text:
Yohannes Christian "Chris" John, born on 14 September 1979 in Banjarnegara, Indonesia, is a former professional boxer who competed from 1998 to 2013. Nicknamed "The Dragon," he held the World Boxing Association (WBA) featherweight title from 2004 to 2009, followed by the WBA Super featherweight title from 2009 to 2013. His near-decade-long reign as champion was the second longest in featherweight history, surpassed only by Johnny Kilbane. John successfully defended his title 16 times, the second most in featherweight history after Eusebio Pedroza. He is the fourth Indonesian boxer to win a world title, following Ellyas Pical, Nico Thomas, and Muhammad Rachman.

John’s father, Johan Tjahjadi, a former amateur boxer, introduced him to boxing at age five, inspiring him with stories of his own fights. By his teenage years, John had become an amateur champion in Banjarnegara. In 1997, renowned trainer Sutan Rambing recruited him to his gym in Semarang, where John trained until 2004. John turned professional in 1997, winning his debut fight by knockout. Early in his career, he earned his signature nickname after initially being called "The Thin Man." A significant early victory came in his sixth bout, when he knocked out national featherweight champion Muhammad Afaridzi in a 12-round fight, despite being knocked down twice in the first round.

John soon captured the PABA featherweight title, leading to a world title shot against Oscar León of Colombia in 2003. Despite León’s physical advantages in height and reach, John won by split decision. He defended his title against notable opponents, including Derrick Gainer (2005), Juan Manuel Márquez (2006), and Hiroyuki Enoki (2008). His 2006 fight against Márquez, a four-time world champion, was particularly notable, as Márquez’s team disputed the unanimous decision. In 2009, he moved up to the super featherweight division, defeating Rocky Juarez in a rematch after their first fight ended in a draw. He later defended his title against Daud Yordan, Shoji Kimura, and Chonlatarn Piriyapinyo before suffering a technical draw against Satoshi Hosono due to a headbutt.

John’s reign ended on 6 December 2013 when he lost to Simpiwe Vetyeka, retiring after the sixth round. This marked his first career loss and the end of his 10-year title reign. After retiring, he pursued business ventures with his wife and appeared in TV commercials and motivational programs.

Beyond boxing, John was also a member of Indonesia’s national wushu team, earning multiple medals, including golds at the 1997 Southeast Asian Games in Jakarta and the 1996 Indonesian National Olympics. In 2012, the WBA named him Fighter of the Decade for the 2000s, an honor previously held by Roy Jones Jr. Throughout his career, John was trained by his father (1984–1997), Sutan Rambing (1997–2004), and Craig Christian (2005–2013). His professional record stands as a testament to his dominance in the featherweight division.

title: Amelia Earhart
text:
Amelia Mary Earhart, born on July 24, 1897, in Atchison, Kansas, was an American aviation pioneer who became one of the most celebrated female pilots of the 20th century. She disappeared over the Pacific Ocean on July 2, 1937, while attempting to become the first woman to fly around the world, and was officially declared dead on January 5, 1939. Throughout her life, Earhart embraced women's rights, promoted commercial aviation, and set multiple flying records. Her mysterious disappearance has fueled enduring public interest and conspiracy theories.

Earhart was the second child of Samuel "Edwin" Stanton Earhart and Amelia "Amy" Otis Earhart, and she grew up with a rebellious, adventurous spirit. From a young age, she defied traditional gender roles, climbing trees, hunting with a rifle, and building makeshift roller coasters with her sister, Grace. After her father's financial struggles and her grandmother’s death, the family’s resources diminished, forcing Earhart to seek her own path. She attended several schools, including Hyde Park High School and briefly studied at Ogontz School and Columbia University, but never completed a formal degree.

In 1917, during World War I, Earhart worked as a nurse’s aide in Toronto, Canada, where she cared for wounded soldiers and developed an interest in aviation. After contracting the Spanish flu in 1918, she spent nearly a year recovering from pneumonia and sinusitis, which would later affect her flying career. In 1920, she took her first airplane ride, which sparked her lifelong passion for flying. She saved money to take flying lessons and, in 1921, began training with instructor Neta Snook. Six months later, she purchased a used Kinner Airster biplane, which she named "The Canary." On October 22, 1922, she set a world altitude record for female pilots by flying to 14,000 feet. In 1923, she became the 16th woman in the U.S. to earn a pilot’s license.

Despite financial struggles, Earhart continued flying and advocating for women in aviation. In 1928, she gained international fame as the first woman to cross the Atlantic by airplane, though she was only a passenger on that flight. Four years later, on May 20–21, 1932, she made history as the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic, a 14-hour, 56-minute journey from Newfoundland to Ireland. For this achievement, she was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross. She also became a visiting faculty member at Purdue University, where she encouraged female students to pursue careers in aviation and engineering.

Earhart was an outspoken supporter of women’s rights and the Equal Rights Amendment. She co-founded the Ninety-Nines, an organization for female pilots, and used her celebrity to promote aviation and women’s independence. In 1935, she set another record by flying solo from Hawaii to California. On her final flight in 1937, accompanied by navigator Fred Noonan, she intended to circumnavigate the globe. After taking off from Lae, New Guinea, they vanished near Howland Island in the Pacific. Despite extensive search efforts, neither Earhart, Noonan, nor their Lockheed Electra aircraft were ever found. The most widely accepted theory is that they ran out of fuel and crashed into the ocean.

Earhart’s legacy endures as a symbol of courage and ambition. She was posthumously inducted into the National Aviation Hall of Fame (1968) and the National Women’s Hall of Fame (1973). Numerous memorials, including airports, schools, and a U.S. postage stamp, honor her contributions. Her life has inspired countless books, films, and documentaries, cementing her status as one of aviation’s most iconic figures.

title: Alfred Hitchcock
text:
least some ambiguity, but the studio insisted on a clear resolution. The film’s suspenseful storytelling and innovative techniques, such as the use of close-ups and dramatic lighting, earned it critical and commercial success. *The Lodger* is now considered a landmark in the thriller genre, laying the foundation for Hitchcock’s later works.

In 1929, Hitchcock directed *Blackmail*, which became the first British "talkie" (sound film). Though the production was fraught with technical difficulties, the film was a breakthrough in British cinema, showcasing Hitchcock’s ability to adapt to new technologies. The film’s famous scene in which a murder weapon—a knife—is magnified in a close-up became a signature Hitchcockian technique.

Throughout the 1930s, Hitchcock continued to refine his craft, directing a series of successful thrillers that solidified his reputation as a master of suspense. *The Man Who Knew Too Much* (1934), *The 39 Steps* (1935), and *The Lady Vanishes* (1938) are now regarded as classics of British cinema. These films featured intricate plots, memorable characters, and Hitchcock’s trademark visual and narrative techniques, such as the use of mistaken identities, wrongful accusations, and suspenseful pacing. *The 39 Steps* in particular introduced the "MacGuffin" concept—a plot device that drives the story but is ultimately irrelevant to the characters’ emotional journey.

By the late 1930s, Hitchcock’s international fame grew, and in 1939, he was persuaded by producer David O. Selznick to move to Hollywood. This transition marked a new phase in his career, as he began working with major American stars and studios. His first Hollywood film, *Rebecca* (1940), based on Daphne du Maurier’s novel, won the Academy Award for Best Picture, though Hitchcock was not recognized as Best Director. The film’s atmospheric storytelling and psychological depth set the tone for his subsequent Hollywood works.

Hitchcock’s Hollywood career produced some of his most celebrated films, including *Foreign Correspondent* (1940), *Suspicion* (1941), *Shadow of a Doubt* (1943), and *Notorious* (1946). *Shadow of a Doubt*, which he considered his personal favorite, explores themes of innocence and moral corruption within a seemingly idyllic small town. *Notorious*, starring Cary Grant and Ingrid Bergman, is noted for its complex romantic and espionage plot, as well as its groundbreaking use of deep-focus cinematography.

In the 1950s and 1960s, Hitchcock continued to innovate, directing films that pushed the boundaries of suspense and psychological drama. *Strangers on a Train* (1951) features a chilling premise involving a murder pact, while *Dial M for Murder* (1954) and *Rope* (1948) experimented with limited camera movements and long takes. *Vertigo* (1958), starring James Stewart, is a haunting exploration of obsession and identity, while *North by Northwest* (1959) is a stylish thriller with iconic set pieces, including the crop-duster scene.

Hitchcock’s later works, such as *The Birds* (1963) and *Marnie* (1964), delved into more unconventional themes, blending psychological realism with surreal elements. *Psycho* (1960), with its shocking twists and revolutionary editing, remains one of his most famous films, redefining the horror-suspense genre.

Throughout his career, Hitchcock became a cultural icon, known for his cameos in his own films, his witty interviews, and his television series *Alfred Hitchcock Presents*. He worked with leading stars of the era, including Cary Grant, James Stewart, Grace Kelly, and Ingrid Bergman, forming creative partnerships that enhanced his films. His contributions to cinema earned him numerous accolades, including BAFTA’s Fellowship in 1971 and the AFI Life Achievement Award in 1979. He was knighted in 1979, just four months before his death in 1980.

Hitchcock’s legacy endures, with many of his films preserved in the U.S. National Film Registry. In 2012, *Vertigo* surpassed *Citizen Kane* as the greatest film of all time in a British Film Institute poll, a testament to his enduring influence. His techniques, themes, and storytelling prowess continue to inspire filmmakers worldwide.

title: Tom Coburn
text:
Thomas Allen Coburn (1948–2020) was an American politician and physician who served as a U.S. senator from Oklahoma from 2005 to 2015 and as a U.S. representative from 1995 to 2001. A fiscal and social conservative, Coburn was known for his opposition to deficit spending, pork-barrel projects, and abortion, earning the nickname "Dr. No" for frequently blocking federal spending bills. He was also a strong advocate for term limits, gun rights, and the death penalty while opposing same-sex marriage and embryonic stem cell research.

Born in Casper, Wyoming, Coburn grew up in Oklahoma and graduated with a degree in accounting from Oklahoma State University. After working in manufacturing, he pursued a medical degree, graduating with honors from the University of Oklahoma Medical School in 1983. He then opened a private obstetrics practice in Muskogee, where he treated over 15,000 patients and delivered 4,000 babies. A devout Southern Baptist, Coburn served as a deacon in his local church.

Coburn entered politics in 1994, winning election to the U.S. House of Representatives as part of the Republican Revolution. He was reelected twice but chose not to seek a fourth term, adhering to his self-imposed three-term limit. During his House tenure, Coburn gained a reputation as a conservative maverick, often clashing with Speaker Newt Gingrich over what he saw as the party's drift from its core principles. He authored legislation to combat AIDS, expand rural healthcare access, and allow cheaper medication imports from Canada. In 2000, he endorsed conservative activist Alan Keyes in the Republican presidential primaries.

After a brief hiatus, Coburn returned to politics in 2004, winning a U.S. Senate seat. He was reelected in 2010 but announced in 2014 that he would resign early due to a recurrence of prostate cancer. In the Senate, Coburn was a staunch fiscal hawk, often using procedural holds to block bills he deemed wasteful or excessive. Notable examples included holding up a veterans benefits bill and a bill honoring Rachel Carson, which he criticized for promoting "junk science." He also opposed legislation to protect wilderness areas, arguing that funding for such measures was unnecessary.

Coburn faced controversy during his Senate career over a 1990 sterilization procedure he performed on a 20-year-old woman during emergency surgery. The patient later sued, claiming she did not consent, while Coburn maintained he had oral consent. The lawsuit was dismissed, but the incident became a contentious issue in his 2004 Senate campaign. Additionally, Coburn was involved in mediating an affair involving Senator John Ensign, another member of the religious organization The Family. Coburn refused to discuss his role, citing legal privilege as both a physician and a deacon.

After leaving the Senate, Coburn worked with the Manhattan Institute for Policy Research on FDA reform and served as a senior advisor to Citizens for Self-Governance, advocating for a constitutional convention. He died in 2020 at the age of 72. Throughout his career, Coburn remained a vocal advocate for limited government and fiscal responsibility, leaving a lasting impact on conservative politics.

title: Umika Kawashima
text:
Umika Kawashima, born on March 3, 1994, in Saitama Prefecture, is a Japanese actress, voice actress, and singer. She began her career in entertainment at a young age, having been scouted in Shibuya while in sixth grade and subsequently joining Lespros Entertainment. Throughout her career, she has cited actresses Aoi Miyazaki, Yui Aragaki, and Kou Shibasaki as her idols and has expressed a desire to collaborate with singer-songwriter Masaharu Fukuyama. In 2016, she graduated from Meiji University with a degree in psychology from the Faculty of Arts and Letters, balancing her academic pursuits with her growing career in the entertainment industry.

Kawashima gained early recognition as a member of the Japanese girl group 9nine, which she joined in 2007. However, in 2016, she announced her departure from the group to focus solely on her acting career, performing her final concert with 9nine at the "9nine LIVE 2016, BEST 9 Tour." Before her graduation, she had been a member for nine and a half years. Around the same time, she was announced as a regular co-host on the television program *ZIP!*, alongside Masu Taichi. Reflecting on this transition, Kawashima expressed her determination to present an engaging program without mishaps, signaling her commitment to her new role.

As an actress, Kawashima has built an extensive filmography, appearing in numerous television dramas and movies since 2006. Her breakthrough in voice acting came in 2017 when she landed her first leading role in the anime series *Nana Maru San Batsu*. Additionally, she has lent her voice to dubbing roles, most notably as Mavis Dracula in the *Hotel Transylvania* film franchise, appearing in all four installments. Her singing career includes the solo single *"Maji de Koi Suru 5 Byō Mae/Ichigo Iro no Kimochi,"* which was featured on the *Watashi no Yasashikunai Senpai* soundtrack and reached number 46 on the Oricon charts.

Kawashima’s career has been marked by accolades, including the Best Newcomer Award at the 2nd Tokyo Drama Awards in 2009. She also received the Special Prize at the 23rd Japan Best Dressed Eyes Awards in 2010 and was named one of the Best Jewelry Dressers in Japan (in the teens category) in 2013. These awards highlight her versatility and influence in the entertainment industry.

In her personal life, Kawashima has maintained a relatively private profile. However, in December 2024, she and Olympic competitive swimmer Katsumi Nakamura jointly announced their marriage, marking a significant milestone in her life. Through her career and personal growth, Kawashima has demonstrated a balance between her professional ambitions and personal relationships, solidifying her presence in Japanese entertainment. Her journey from a scouted young talent to a accomplished actress, voice actress, and singer reflects her dedication and adaptability in the ever-evolving entertainment landscape.

title: Mamunul Islam
text:
Mamunul Islam Mamun is a prominent Bangladeshi professional footballer, born on 12 December 1988, who has had a distinguished career as a midfielder in both domestic and international football. He played for the Bangladesh national team from 2009 to 2020, serving as captain from 2013 to 2016. Over his career, Mamunul has won five league titles across multiple clubs. He began his professional journey in 2005 with Brothers Union, where he played as a central midfielder and contributed to the team's success in the Dhaka Premier Division League and Federation Cup that year.

In 2008–09, Mamunul moved to Abahani Limited Dhaka, helping them win the league title during his first season. The following year, he joined their arch-rival, Mohammedan SC, and added the Federation Cup and Super Cup to his trophy collection. His tenure at Sheikh Jamal Dhanmondi Club from 2010–11 was particularly successful, as he won his second league title in his debut season with the club. After a brief stint with Muktijoddha Sangsad KC in 2011–12, he transferred to Sheikh Russel KC, where he secured another league title, along with the Federation Cup and Independence Cup in the 2012–13 season.

Mamunul returned to Sheikh Jamal Dhanmondi Club in 2013–14 and led the team as captain, winning back-to-back league titles in 2013–14 and 2014–15. During this period, he also played a short loan spell with Atlético de Kolkata in the inaugural season of the Indian Super League, becoming the only South Asian player outside India to feature in the league's first edition. Despite his strong performances, he did not secure a starting role with the club. His contributions at Sheikh Jamal Dhanmondi Club also included two Federation Cup victories in successive seasons.

In 2016, Mamunul joined his hometown club, Chittagong Abahani, for a record transfer fee of 65 lakh taka, captaining the team in his first season and winning the Independence Cup. After two seasons, he returned to Abahani Limited Dhaka in 2018, where he provided valuable experience to the team. In 2021, he made a comeback to Dhaka Mohammedan SC after an 11-year absence, and later joined Rahmatganj MFS in 2022 to help the struggling club avoid relegation. Mamunul announced his retirement from international football on 6 September 2020.

Throughout his career, Mamunul has been a key figure in Bangladeshi football, earning numerous domestic honors, including multiple league titles, Federation Cups, and an Independence Cup. He also played a pivotal role in Bangladesh's U-23 team, helping them win gold at the 2010 South Asian Games. His leadership and talent have made him one of the most decorated midfielders in Bangladesh's football history.

title: Grayston Burgess
text:
Grayston Burgess, born on 7 April 1932 in Cheriton, Kent, and passing away on 6 March 2019, was a notable English countertenor and conductor whose career spanned decades. His early musical training began as a chorister in the choir of Canterbury Cathedral during World War II, a formative experience that shaped his later work in choral music. After his time at Canterbury, he attended Cheltenham College before securing a choral scholarship to sing in the prestigious Choir of King's College, Cambridge, under the renowned conductor Boris Ord. This period solidified his reputation as a talented vocalist and set the stage for his future contributions to early music and choral performance.

Burgess was associated with several prominent early music ensembles, including the Purcell Singers, with whom he performed before founding the Purcell Consort of Voices in 1963. This ensemble became a key platform for his work as both a singer and conductor, specializing in early music and historically informed performances. He also collaborated with the Studio der frühen Musik and the Musica Reservata Ensemble, led by Michael Morrow and John Beckett, further establishing his expertise in Renaissance and Baroque repertoire. One of his notable performances was the premiere of Michael Tippett’s "Songs for Ariel," showcasing his versatility as a countertenor.

In the 1980s, Burgess relocated to rural Herefordshire, where he transitioned into teaching, taking on roles at Ellerslie School in Malvern and later at Malvern College following Ellerslie’s closure. His teaching career produced notable students, including Wendy Nieper, a former member of the Swingle Singers, reflecting his influence as an educator.

Burgess’s impact extended beyond performance and teaching. In 2000, he was invited to form and direct a community choir to commemorate the Millennium, which performed Haydn’s *The Creation*. The choir, later renamed Choir 2000, became a lasting institution, and Burgess remained a guiding force in its development. His dedication to choral music was recognized in 2017 when the *Daily Telegraph* interviewed him for an article on women in British cathedral choirs, highlighting his long-standing contributions to the field. However, the article notably omitted his involvement with the Campaign for the Traditional Cathedral Choir, an organization known for opposing the inclusion of women and girls in cathedral and church choirs, suggesting a divisive aspect of his legacy.

Burgess’s discography reflects his dual roles as soloist and conductor. As a countertenor, he recorded works by John Dowland, among others, while his leadership of the Purcell Consort of Voices resulted in recordings such as *Music of Albert: Prince of Saxe, Coburg und Gotha*. These recordings preserved his interpretations of early music and his commitment to historical performance practices.

Throughout his life, Grayston Burgess was a significant figure in the world of early music and choral performance, leaving a lasting mark as both a performer and an educator. His work with ensembles like the Purcell Consort of Voices, his teaching, and his leadership of Choir 2000 underscored his dedication to preserving and promoting early music traditions. Despite controversies surrounding his associations, his contributions to choral music remain widely recognized.

title: Richard Kuklinski
text:
Richard Leonard Kuklinski, also known as the Iceman, was an American criminal who led a burglary ring in New Jersey and committed at least five confirmed murders between 1980 and 1984. His nickname came from his method of freezing the body of one victim to disguise the time of death. Kuklinski lived a double life in the suburb of Dumont with his wife and children, who claimed to be unaware of his criminal activities. His modus operandi involved luring men to meetings with promises of business deals, then killing them for money. He also murdered two associates to prevent them from becoming informants.

Law enforcement first became suspicious of Kuklinski when investigating his burglary gang, which led to his arrest in December 1986 after an 18-month undercover operation. In 1988, he was convicted of four murders and sentenced to life imprisonment. Later, in 2003, he received an additional 30-year sentence after confessing to the 1980 murder of an NYPD detective. During interviews after his conviction, Kuklinski claimed to have murdered between 100 and 200 men, though these claims have not been corroborated. Law enforcement estimates his actual victim count may be as low as 15. He also claimed ties to the Mafia, including involvement in high-profile murders like Jimmy Hoffa’s, but these claims are widely disputed.

Kuklinski’s childhood was marked by severe abuse. Born in Jersey City in 1935, he was the second of four children to a violent, alcoholic father and an abusive mother. His older brother died from his father’s beatings, and his younger brother was later convicted of rape and murder. Kuklinski’s upbringing left deep scars, and he later rejected his Catholic faith. As an adult, his personality was described as volatile, alternating between affectionate and violent. His wife, Barbara, endured his abuse, fearing for her safety and that of their children. Despite his criminal lifestyle, neighbors believed he was a successful businessman.

Kuklinski’s criminal career began with distributing pirated pornography and films in the 1960s, which led to connections with the Gambino crime family. His first confirmed murder was in 1980, when he killed George Malliband, a man who had $27,000 on him, by shooting him five times and storing his body in a drum. In 1982, he killed pharmacist Paul Hoffman after luring him to a meeting, beating him to death with a tire iron. Later that year, he poisoned and strangled Gary Smith, a burglary associate, fearing he would inform on him. In 1983, he killed Daniel Deppner, another associate, and disposed of his body near a wooded area. His final confirmed victim was Louis Masgay, whom he shot in 1981 and froze before dumping his body in 1983, earning him the nickname "Iceman."

Kuklinski’s claims of additional murders, including using unconventional methods like a crossbow and cyanide spray, remain unverified. His life and crimes were the subject of documentaries, biographies, and a 2012 film. He died in prison in 2006, leaving behind a legacy of violence and controversy over his true number of victims.

title: David Oyite-Ojok
text:
David Oyite-Ojok was a prominent Ugandan military officer whose career was deeply intertwined with the political upheavals of his country. Born on 15 April 1940 in Lira District, he was an ethnic Lango who began his military service in 1963 under President Milton Obote’s first government. By 1965, he was already teaching officer cadets in Jinja, and later that year, he was transferred to Army Headquarters, where he held key administrative roles, including Deputy Assistant Adjutant and Quartermaster General. In 1970, while Obote was still in power, Oyite-Ojok was appointed Assistant Military Secretary, a position that involved strategic planning and policy oversight. He later received military training in Great Britain.

When Idi Amin seized power in a 1971 coup, Oyite-Ojok fled to Tanzania, where he joined Obote’s exile forces. During this time, he developed a legendary reputation in Uganda, with stories circulating about his daring exploits, including reportedly infiltrating Kampala to party at nightclubs and leaving the bill for Amin to pay. Amin allegedly placed a $70,000 bounty on his head. In 1972, Oyite-Ojok led a failed rebel invasion of Uganda, after which Obote reorganized his forces, placing Oyite-Ojok in command of a naval operation on Lake Victoria to support the rebellion.

In 1978, when Tanzania invaded Uganda, sparking the Uganda-Tanzania War, Oyite-Ojok emerged as a key military leader. He commanded Obote’s private army, Kikosi Maalum, and later became chief of staff of the Uganda National Liberation Army (UNLA), the coalition force that, with Tanzanian support, overthrew Amin. His tactical leadership was credited with major victories, including the Battle of Lukaya and the Fall of Kampala.

After Amin’s removal, Oyite-Ojok became a member of the Military Commission, a powerful group within the Uganda National Liberation Front (UNLF) that governed Uganda. Alongside figures like Yoweri Museveni, Paulo Muwanga, and Tito Okello, he played a central role in the post-Amin transition. However, his loyalty to Obote and his northern tribal affiliations fueled political tensions. He ensured the UNLA remained dominated by northerners, particularly Langi and Acholi soldiers, which intensified ethnic rivalries. His influence was so great that when President Yusuf Lule tried to reduce his power in 1980, the Military Commission deposed Lule and installed Godfrey Binaisa as a figurehead. Later, when Binaisa attempted to dismiss Oyite-Ojok, the Military Commission removed Binaisa, consolidating power under a new Presidential Commission.

Oyite-Ojok actively campaigned for Obote’s return, using his military prestige to mobilize northern support. After Obote’s victory in the 1980 elections, Oyite-Ojok remained Army Chief of Staff, leading brutal campaigns against Museveni’s National Resistance Army (NRA) and other rebel groups. His tactics included mass arrests and executions in Kampala and the infamous "Luwero Triangle" massacres, where thousands of civilians were killed. By 1983, the UNLA had largely suppressed the rebellion, but internal military tensions were rising, particularly between the Langi and Acholi soldiers.

On 2 December 1983, Oyite-Ojok died in a helicopter crash in Nakasongola District. The NRA claimed responsibility, while Obote’s government blamed mechanical failure, fueling speculation that Obote may have orchestrated his death due to growing discontent. His death had significant political consequences, as it intensified divisions within the military. Obote’s decision to replace him with a junior Langi officer, Smith Apon-Achak, further alienated Acholi officers, contributing to their eventual overthrow of Obote in 1985.

Despite his controversial role in the conflict, Oyite-Ojok was later honored as a national hero by Museveni’s government, a recognition of his pivotal role in Uganda’s military history. His life exemplified the deep political and ethnic divisions that shaped Uganda’s post-Amin era, leaving a complex and enduring legacy.

title: Thomas Piketty
text:
Thomas Piketty is a prominent French economist born on 7 May 1971 in Clichy, a suburb of Paris. His parents were once involved with a Trotskyist group and the May 1968 protests but had moved away from those political views before his birth. After a visit to the Soviet Union in 1991, Piketty became a firm supporter of capitalism, private property, and free markets. He excelled academically, earning a scientific Baccalauréat and later entering the prestigious École Normale Supérieure (ENS) at 18 to study mathematics and economics. At 22, he completed a PhD in wealth redistribution, earning the French Economics Association’s award for the best thesis of the year. During this time, he studied at the London School of Economics (LSE) and the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales (EHESS) under Roger Guesnerie and met economist Daron Acemoglu.

Piketty’s academic career began at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he taught from 1993 to 1995. He later joined the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and became a professor at EHESS in 2000. His work focuses on public economics, particularly income and wealth inequality. His 2013 book, *Capital in the Twenty-First Century*, became a bestseller, arguing that wealth inequality tends to increase over time due to the rate of capital return exceeding economic growth. The book proposes a progressive global tax on wealth as a solution. Piketty’s 2019 follow-up, *Capital and Ideology*, examines historical ideologies that justify inequality and advocates for policies like wealth redistribution. His 2022 book, *A Brief History of Equality*, is a shorter work aimed at a general audience, discussing the evolution of wealth redistribution from 1780 to 2020.

Throughout his career, Piketty has been politically active, supporting socialist candidates in France, including Ségolène Royal in 2007 and François Hollande in 2012. He later advised Benoît Hamon in the 2017 presidential campaign, advocating for renegotiating the Fiscal Stability Treaty to create a more democratic EU governance structure. He has also been involved with the British Labour Party, serving on its Economic Advisory Committee under Jeremy Corbyn in 2015 before resigning in 2016 due to disagreements over the EU referendum campaign. In 2015, he rejected the French Legion of Honour, stating that he did not believe the government should decide who is honourable.

Piketty’s research uses historical and statistical methods to analyze wealth inequality, particularly in France and the US. His work has shown that high-income earners in France took more than half of the country’s total income in 2012, the highest level recorded in a century. He argues that progressive taxation after World War II reduced inequality, but tax cuts since the 1990s have allowed wealth to accumulate again, leading to what he calls "patrimonial capitalism," where a few families dominate wealth. His studies also challenge the Kuznets curve, which suggests inequality decreases as economies develop, by showing that post-war inequality reductions were due to progressive taxation rather than economic forces.

Beyond his core research, Piketty has explored other topics, including education disparities, pension reform, and political party dynamics. He has argued that both left- and right-wing parties in the West have been captured by elites, coining the terms "Brahmin Left" and "Merchant Right." His work has earned him numerous accolades, including the Yrjö Jahnsson Award in 2013 and the British Academy Medal in 2014.

Piketty currently holds positions at the School for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences (EHESS), the Paris School of Economics (PSE), and the London School of Economics (LSE). He continues to teach and conduct research, with a focus on inter-disciplinary approaches to inequality. His personal life includes a former relationship with politician Aurélie Filippetti, who filed a complaint of domestic violence against him in 2009, though the details of the case remain unclear.

title: Chris Cuomo
text:
Christopher Charles Cuomo, born on August 9, 1970, in Queens, New York, is an American journalist and anchor at NewsNation. The son of former New York Governor Mario Cuomo and Matilda Cuomo, and the brother of another former New York Governor, Andrew Cuomo, Chris Cuomo comes from a prominent political family. His paternal grandparents were from Nocera Inferiore and Tramonti in Italy, while his maternal grandparents were from Sicily.

Cuomo earned his undergraduate degree from Yale University and later obtained a Juris Doctor from Fordham University School of Law, becoming a licensed attorney. His early career included work as a correspondent and political analyst for Fox News and Fox Broadcast Network’s *Fox Files*, where he covered controversial social issues. He described himself as an objective journalist, stating that his personal opinions were irrelevant to his reporting.

From 2006 to 2009, Cuomo served as the news anchor for *Good Morning America*, covering major domestic and international breaking news, including the Virginia Tech shooting, the 2009 Fort Hood shooting, and the Haiti earthquake. His investigative work led to policy changes, such as a recall of over 150,000 BMW vehicles after a tip from a viewer. He also hosted digital programs, including *Cuomo on the Case* and *Focus on Faith*, and reported on social issues like heroin addiction and homeless teens.

In 2013, Cuomo joined CNN, co-hosting the morning show *New Day* before moving to prime time with *Cuomo Prime Time* in 2018. He also hosted a radio show, *Let’s Get After It*, on SiriusXM. In 2019, he was involved in a public altercation after a heckler called him "Fredo," a reference to a weak character in *The Godfather*, which Cuomo compared to a racial slur. He later apologized for his response.

Controversy arose in 2021 when it was revealed that Cuomo had advised his brother, then-Governor Andrew Cuomo, on handling sexual harassment allegations. CNN initially called his involvement inappropriate but took no action. However, further reports showed that Cuomo had used his media connections to gather information on accusers, leading to his indefinite suspension and eventual termination in December 2021. He later filed a $125 million lawsuit against CNN, claiming defamation.

Cuomo also faced sexual misconduct allegations from former colleagues, including a 2021 claim by Shelley Ross, who accused him of inappropriate behavior. Another former colleague later accused him of sexual assault, though Cuomo denied the allegations.

After leaving CNN, Cuomo launched a podcast, *The Chris Cuomo Project*, and in 2022, he joined NewsNation, where he hosts a primetime show. He has interviewed high-profile figures, including Kanye West, and has emphasized a more neutral approach to journalism. His career has earned him multiple Emmy nominations, a News Emmy for his *Good Morning America* profile of poet Mattie Stepanek, and awards like the Polk, Peabody, and Edward R. Murrow Awards.

Personal life includes his marriage to Cristina Greeven, an editor, with whom he has three children. They reside in Manhattan and Southampton. In 2020, Cuomo contracted COVID-19, experiencing hallucinations and later reporting long COVID symptoms. He remains active in journalism, continuing to work in media despite past controversies.

title: Krystyna Szczepańska
text:
Krystyna Szczepańska, born on 18 August 1950 in Kraków, is a Polish stage and costume designer with a notable career in both film and theatre. She comes from a family with strong ties to Poland’s history and culture. Her father, Piotr Szczepański, was a lawyer and graduate of Jan Kazimierz University, while her mother, Stanisława Żółtańska, was a Russian language teacher. Both of her parents were members of the Home Army, the Polish resistance movement during World War II. Szczepańska is the second child in her family, with an elder sister, Alicja, who is also a lawyer. Her personal life includes a marriage to director Andrzej Maj, with whom she collaborated on numerous projects, primarily designing sets and costumes for his theatrical productions. Together, they had two daughters: Magdalena, who follows in her mother’s footsteps as a costume and set designer, primarily working in the advertising industry, and Elizabeth.

Szczepańska’s professional work spans both television and theatre. In television, she contributed to numerous productions as a set designer, including *My wciąż spieszący* (1981), *Kocham cię za to, że cię kochać muszę* (1981), *Znana nasza* (1982), *Milczeć pogodnie* (1982), *Droga do Czarnolasu* (1983), *Wiersze i krajobrazy* (1984), *Piękność z Amherst* (1984), *Obszar swobody* (1984), *Nad wodą wielką i czystą* (1985), *Twarze Witkacego czyli regulamin firmy portretowej* (1986), *Dwie wigilie* (1986), *Trąd w pałacu sprawiedliwości* (1987), *Harnasie* (1987), *Dzieje kultury polskiej* (1988), and *Koty? Koty!* (1991). She also worked as a costume designer for *Nad wodą wielką i czystą* (1985) and *Harnasie* (1987), as well as an interior decorator for *Kornblumenblau* (1988).

In theatre, Szczepańska’s work was closely tied to her husband’s directorial projects. Her stage design contributions include *Niebezpieczne związki* (1979) at the Ludwik Solski Theatre in Tarnów, *Jednorożec z gwiazd* (1982) and *Historia, czyli tu wcale nie chodzi o Mozarta* (1982) at the Stefan Jaracz Theatre in Łódź. She also designed the set for *Ozimina* (1983) at the same theatre. As a costume designer, she worked on *Pornografia* (1985), again at the Stefan Jaracz Theatre, directed by Maj.

Szczepańska’s career reflects a deep engagement with Polish cultural and artistic traditions, particularly through her collaborations with her husband and her contributions to both television and theatre. Her work often involved creating immersive visual experiences, whether through elaborate stage sets or intricate costumes. Over time, she emigrated to Vancouver, where she continues to be part of the broader Polish diaspora. Her family’s legacy, her professional partnerships, and her artistic contributions have solidified her place in Poland’s cultural history.

title: Adnan Sami
text:
Adnan Sami Khan, born on 15 August 1969 in London, England, is a renowned Indian singer, musician, composer, actor, and pianist. He is celebrated for his ability to perform both Indian and Western music in multiple languages, including Hindi, Urdu, English, Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam. Recognized as the first musician to blend santoor and Indian classical music with the piano, Sami has been praised by *Keyboard* magazine as the "fastest keyboard player in the world" and the "keyboard discovery of the nineties." His contributions to music earned him the prestigious Padma Shri, India’s fourth-highest civilian award, in 2020.

Sami was raised and educated in the United Kingdom, where he attended Rugby School and later obtained a law degree from King’s College London, qualifying as a barrister from Lincoln’s Inn. His musical journey began at age five when he started playing the piano, and by nine, he had composed his first piece. Influenced by santoor maestro Pandit Shivkumar Sharma and encouraged by legendary singer Asha Bhosle, Sami dedicated himself to music. As a teenager, he gained international acclaim after a performance on Swedish television, where he was hailed for his speed and skill on the keyboard. At sixteen, he wrote a song for famine-stricken Ethiopia, earning a special UNICEF award.

With a career spanning over three decades, Sami has won numerous international accolades, including the Nigar Award, Bolan Academy Award, and Graduate Award. He is the youngest recipient of the Naushad Music Award, previously given to legends like Lata Mangeshkar and Khayam. His debut single, "Run for His Life" (1986), reached number one in the Middle East, followed by hits like "Talk to Me" and "Hot Summer Day." His first album, *The One & Only* (1989), featured collaborations with tabla maestro Zakir Hussain. *Raag Time* (1991) marked his first vocal solo album, while *Kabhi To Nazar Milao* (2000), a collaboration with Asha Bhosle, became a massive commercial success, selling over 4 million copies in India. His 2002 album *Tera Chehra* broke sales records, becoming the best-selling Indian album of all time in the U.S. and Canada, and remained at the top of Indian charts for over a year.

Sami has composed music for several films, including *Sargam* (1995), *Ajnabee* (2001), and *Bajrangi Bhaijaan* (2015), where he also made a cameo appearance. His song "Tu Sirf Mera Mehboob" from *Ajnabee* was a massive hit, and he collaborated with A.R. Rahman on the song "Aye Udi Udi" for *Saathiya* (2002). Beyond film music, he has performed for international events, including the 2003 Cricket World Cup, and has been a judge on popular reality shows like *Sa Re Ga Ma Pa L'il Champs*.

Despite facing health challenges, including lymphoedema and severe obesity, Sami underwent a remarkable transformation, losing 130 kg. He has performed for royalty and heads of state, including the King of Sweden and King Hussein of Jordan, and sold out Wembley Stadium twice in 2003, earning a place in the *Limca Book of Records*. In 2016, he became an Indian citizen after residing in India for over a decade.

Sami’s personal life has been marked by two divorces, followed by his marriage to Roya Sami Khan in 2010. He has a son, Azaan, and a daughter, Medina. Known for his romantic and soulful music, he remains a revered figure in the Indian music industry, often referred to as the "Sultan of Music."

title: Ki Fitzgerald
text:
Ki Fitzgerald, born Kiley McPhail, is an English DJ, musician, songwriter, and record producer. He is also known by the professional name Azteck. Fitzgerald was born in Rotterdam, Netherlands, to British parents and moved to Kent, England, at the age of six. His father, Scott Fitzgerald, is a well-known singer who achieved international fame with the hit "If I Had Words" and represented the UK at the Eurovision Song Contest in 1988. Ki Fitzgerald began his career as a founding member of the pop rock band Busted, which he joined in 2000. However, he left the group in 2001. In 2008, he made an unsuccessful legal claim for copyright ownership of several Busted songs, including "Year 3000," "What I Go to School For," and "Sleeping with the Light On," which he had previously signed away in 2003.

In 2007, Fitzgerald formed the band Eyes Wide Open and secured a publishing deal with Music Copyright Solutions. The band made their debut at the GWR Fiesta, performing in front of 40,000 people, and later toured the UK. The lineup included Fitzgerald on vocals and guitar, Tom Warner on lead guitar, TK on bass, Pat Garvery on drums, and Will Farquarson on guitar, who later joined the band Bastille. Despite their early success, the band disbanded while recording their debut album with producer Steve Lironi, known for his work with Bon Jovi, and mixer Simon Gogerly.

In 2015, Fitzgerald signed an artist deal with producer RedOne and his label 2101/Capital Records, joining RedOne’s writing group, Team Red. His first release under this collaboration was "Come Follow," a song featuring vocals by KiFi and produced with Dutch DJ duo Sunnery James & Ryan Marciano, which was released through Spinnin' Records in February 2015. Fitzgerald has since become a prominent vocalist in the EDM genre, featuring on tracks such as "Shine a Light" by Hardwell and Wildstylez, "Steal the Moon" by DubVision, "Best Part of Me" by Firebeatz and DubVision, and "Into the Sunset" by Headhunterz, which appeared on shows like *Ellen DeGeneres* and *Dancing with the Stars*. He has also worked with major artists like Armin van Buuren, Dash Berlin, and others on upcoming releases.

In October 2011, Fitzgerald signed with Global Talent Publishing to focus on songwriting for other artists. He quickly established himself as a successful songwriter and producer, working with a diverse range of musicians. Notable collaborations include writing and producing tracks for Lawson, for whom he contributed to four UK top 10 singles: "When She Was Mine" (UK No. 4), "Standing in the Dark" (UK No. 6), "Broken Hearted" featuring B.o.B (UK No. 6), and "Roads." He also co-wrote several other songs on Lawson’s debut album, *Chapman Square*, and its re-release, *Chapman Square – Special Edition (Chapter II)*. Fitzgerald worked on *Word of Mouth*, the third and final album by The Wanted, co-writing "Summer Alive" and "Heart Break Story."

He co-wrote the debut single "Lipstick" by Sophia Del Carmen, featuring Pitbull, alongside RedOne. For Lawson’s second album, *Perspective*, Fitzgerald co-wrote 11 tracks, including the singles "Money" and "Under the Sun." Additionally, he contributed to Galantis’ singles "Hunter" and "San Francisco," the latter featuring Sofia Carson. He also co-wrote "When I Grow Up" for Dimitri Vegas & Like Mike, featuring Wiz Khalifa, and collaborated on "Faded" by Sweater Beats and Icona Pop. In 2018, he co-wrote "Monsters" for Saara Aalto, who performed it at the Eurovision Song Contest representing Finland. More recently, he co-wrote and provided vocals for Armin van Buuren’s 2019 single "Turn It Up." Fitzgerald’s extensive work in songwriting and production has solidified his reputation as a versatile and influential figure in the music industry.

title: Rangi Te Kanawa
text:
Rangituatahi Te Kanawa, also known by her married name Warnes, is a New Zealand textile conservator and weaver who has made significant contributions to the preservation of Māori art and heritage. Born into a family with deep ties to Māori craft traditions, she is the daughter of Diggeress Te Kanawa and the granddaughter of the renowned weaver Dame Rangimarie Hetet. Her affiliations extend to the Ngāti Maniapoto iwi, further grounding her work in cultural significance.

Te Kanawa’s career in textile conservation began with a scholarship from the Department of Internal Affairs, which supported her training in the field. The Aotearoa Moananui a Kiwa Weavers committee recognized the importance of having Māori professionals involved in the conservation of Māori textile artefacts held in museums and cultural institutions. Her early training included a stint in Canberra, followed by a year of pre-training at the conservation unit of the National Museum in Wellington.
