His versatility extends beyond Hindustani music, as he has also accompanied Carnatic performers such as T. N. Krishnan, N. Ramani, U. Shrinivas, and Lalgudi Krishnan. Beyond the classical realm, Kalyanpur has worked with global artists, including touring with A.R. Rahman for the JAI HO World Tour and contributing to recordings with Keith Richards of The Rolling Stones on Katy Perry’s "Legendary Lovers" from her album *Prism*.

Kalyanpur’s contributions to music have been recognized with numerous accolades, including the "TOP" Grade Artist status from All India Radio, the 'Taal – Mani' award from Sur Singar Samiti, the Vidyasagar Award from ITC, and the Sangeet Visharad. He has also received the National Scholarship for Advanced Training from the Government of India and was awarded the prestigious Pandit Jasraj Competition by the Vedic Heritage Center in Long Island, New York.

His performances have taken him to prestigious international festivals, such as the Orient Arts Festival in Estonia, the Edinburgh Festival in Scotland (2003), the Earagal Arts Festival in Ireland, the Jazz Yatra in Mumbai, and the Great Lakes Folk Festival in Lansing, Michigan. Additionally, he has participated in the Saptak Festival, further showcasing his artistry on prominent stages.

Kalyanpur’s influence extends beyond live performances, as he is actively engaged in sharing his knowledge through platforms like the New England School of Music. His presence on social media, including an official website, MySpace, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and YouTube, reflects his commitment to connecting with a global audience. Through his dedication to the tabla and his collaborations across musical genres, Aditya Kalyanpur has established himself as a distinguished figure in the world of Indian classical and contemporary music.

title: Zewde Gebre-Sellassie
text:
Dejazmatch Zewde Gebre-Sellassie was an Ethiopian nobleman, historian, and former deputy prime minister of Ethiopia, born on 12 October 1926 in the village of Galdu, near Addis Ababa. His father, Dejazmatch Gebre Selassie Baria Gabr, was a governor, and his mother, Leult Wolete Israel Seyoum, came from a prominent family, including his grandfather, Ras Seyum Mengesha. His sister was Leult Ijigayehou Asfa Wossen, and he married Woizero Alem Tsehai Araya. Zewde received his early education under a tutor in Addis Ababa before attending schools in Jerusalem and Cairo during Ethiopia’s Fascist occupation. After Ethiopia’s liberation, he studied at Haile Selassie I Secondary School in Addis Ababa, then pursued English literature at the University of Exeter. He later completed legal training at St. Anthony’s College, Oxford, becoming a senior member from 1963 to 1971 and being called to the Bar at Lincoln’s Inn, London. After a period in public service, he returned to Oxford to earn a PhD in history, politics, and economics.

Throughout his career, Zewde held multiple high-ranking positions under Ethiopia’s imperial government. He began as an economic attaché and later headed the Press, Information, and Administration Division at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (1951–53). He then became Director-General of Maritime Affairs (1953–55) and Deputy Minister of Public Works, Transport, and Civil Aviation (1955–57). From 1957 to 1959, he served as Mayor and Governor of Addis Ababa, followed by a posting as Ambassador to Somalia (1959–60). He later became Minister of Justice (1961–63) and Ethiopia’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations (1972–74). In 1974, he briefly served as Minister of the Interior (March–May) and then as Minister of Foreign Affairs (May–November) before the Derg’s violent purge of government officials forced him into exile.

While in exile, Zewde became vice-president of the United Nations Economic and Social Council and later worked as an advisor to the UN Secretariat. He was recognized with national honors from at least seven countries, including the Federal Republic of Germany. In 1998, he joined other prominent Ethiopians in attempting to mediate between Ethiopia and Eritrea during their conflict.

Zewde was also a prolific writer, publishing several books on Ethiopian history and politics. His notable works include *Yohannes IV of Ethiopia: A Political Biography* (1975), *The Conflict of Ethiopia and Eritrea: Causes and Solutions* (2015), *The Blue Nile and its Basins: An Issue of International Concern* (2006), and *The Process of Re-unification of the Ethiopian Empire, 1868-1889* (1971). His academic and diplomatic contributions, along with his historical research, solidified his legacy in Ethiopian and African political and intellectual circles. He passed away on 15 December 2008.

title: Rebecca Romijn
text:
Rebecca Alie O’Connell, known professionally as Rebecca Romijn, is an American actress and former model born on November 6, 1972, in Berkeley, California. Her parents are Elizabeth Romijn, an English as a Second Language instructor, and Jaap Romijn, a custom furniture maker originally from the Netherlands. Romijn’s maternal grandfather was a Presbyterian minister. In her early teens, she struggled with insecurity and scoliosis, which caused her significant pain. Despite her height of 5 feet 11 inches, she played down rumors of being nicknamed the "Jolly Blonde Giant," later admitting she made up the story for humor. She studied music at the University of California, Santa Cruz, before transitioning into modeling, eventually moving to Paris for over three years.

Romijn’s modeling career began in 1991, and she quickly rose to prominence, appearing on the covers of numerous international editions of *Elle*, *Cosmopolitan*, *GQ*, *Esquire*, and *Sports Illustrated*. She worked with major fashion brands such as Escada, Christian Dior, Victoria’s Secret, and Tommy Hilfiger, and walked runways for designers like Giorgio Armani and Anna Molinari alongside supermodels like Naomi Campbell and Cindy Crawford. From 1998 to 2000, she hosted *MTV’s House of Style*, and she frequently appeared on lists of the world’s most beautiful women by publications like *Maxim*, *AskMen*, and *FHM*. She also had a guest role in the animated series *Space Ghost Coast to Coast*.

Her acting career took off in 2000 with her breakout role as Mystique in the *X-Men* film trilogy (2000–2006), a role that required extensive blue body paint and prosthetics. She later reprised the character in an uncredited cameo in *X-Men: First Class* (2011) and is set to return in *Avengers: Doomsday* (2026). She starred in *Femme Fatale* (2002) as dual characters, played Joan in *The Punisher* (2004), and appeared in films like *Rollerball* and *Godsend*. On television, she played Alexis Meade, a transgender character, in *Ugly Betty* (2007–2008) and starred in the short-lived series *Pepper Dennis* and *Eastwick*. She also had recurring roles in *Star Trek: Discovery* (2019) and *Star Trek: Strange New Worlds* (2022–present) as Una Chin-Riley. Additionally, she voiced Lois Lane in the DC Animated Movie Universe and starred as Eve Baird in *The Librarians* (2014–2018). She co-hosted the reality competition show *Skin Wars* and the dating series *The Real Love Boat* (2022–present) with her husband, Jerry O’Connell.

In her personal life, Romijn was married to actor John Stamos from 1998 to 2005, after they met at a Victoria’s Secret show. She later married Jerry O’Connell in 2007, and they have twin daughters born in 2008. Though she resumed using her maiden name, she revealed that she never legally changed it back from Romijn-Stamos. Beyond acting, she has dabbled in music, covering Prince’s "Darling Nikki" and appearing on RuPaul’s album *Realness*. Romijn’s career spans modeling, television, film, and reality TV, showcasing her versatility as an entertainer.

title: Daniel Bedingfield
text:
Daniel John Bedingfield, born on 3 December 1979 in Auckland, New Zealand, is a singer, songwriter, record producer, and actor of New Zealand-British descent. His musical career began in earnest in 2001 with the release of his debut single, "Gotta Get Thru This," which became a number-one hit in the UK. This success was followed by two more UK number-one singles, "If You're Not the One" and "Never Gonna Leave Your Side," all of which were featured on his debut album, *Gotta Get Thru This* (2002). The album, which he recorded at home using digital audio software, became a massive commercial success, selling over 1.6 million copies in the UK alone and more than 4 million worldwide. It reached number two on the UK Albums Chart, establishing Bedingfield as a prominent figure in early 2000s pop music.

In 2004, Bedingfield won a BRIT Award for Best British Male Artist. His second album, *Second First Impression*, was released the same year under Polydor Records, though it failed to match the success of his debut, peaking at number eight in the UK. Despite this, it included two UK Top 20 singles, "Nothing Hurts Like Love" (number three) and "Wrap My Words Around You" (number twelve). The album's third single, "The Way," did not chart as strongly, reaching only number 41. Following this, Bedingfield took an extended hiatus from solo releases but remained active in the music industry, co-writing songs for other artists. Notably, he worked with David Archuleta, Pixie Lott, and K-pop group Spica, co-producing their English-language single "I Did It." He also contributed to tracks by Tessanne Chin and The Raw Men Empire in Israel, as well as dancehall artist Busy Signal in Jamaica.

In 2012, Bedingfield returned to music with the single "Rocks Off," followed by the EP *Stop the Traffik – Secret Fear*. The EP featured experimental tracks and was supported by a controversial music video for the single "Secret Fear." That same year, he began judging on *The X Factor New Zealand*, mentoring the winning act, Jackie Thomas. He also appeared on *The X Factor Around the World* in 2013, performing his hits and collaborating with other judges. Beyond music, Bedingfield acted in the West End production of *The War of the Worlds* in 2016, playing The Artilleryman.

Bedingfield has also been involved in activism, particularly through his mother's organization, Global Angels, which focuses on humanitarian efforts. He helped launch the Stop the Traffik coalition, an anti-slavery campaign, and has used his platform to raise awareness about modern-day slavery. His personal life has included challenges, including a near-fatal car accident in 2004 that left him with severe injuries. He has also been open about being autistic.

As of 2024, Bedingfield announced a UK tour, reaffirming his enduring presence in the music industry. His career has spanned hit songs, songwriting collaborations, television appearances, and theatrical roles, making him a versatile figure in entertainment. His debut album remains a defining work of early 2000s pop, while his later projects showcase his continued creativity and adaptability.

title: Khalid Mahmood Mithu
text:
Khalid Mahmood Mithu (1960–2016) was a prominent Bangladeshi filmmaker and painter who made significant contributions to both the arts and cinema. Born in Dhaka in 1960, he came from a family deeply involved in the arts. His mother, Begum Momtaz Hossain Mithu, was a scriptwriter, and his uncle, Alamgir Kabir, was a well-known film director, which likely influenced his own career path. Mithu pursued higher education at the University of Dhaka, earning a Master of Fine Arts (MFA) in 1986 from the Faculty of Fine Arts.

His career in film began with the play *Dhusor Album*, which he directed in 1993. However, his most notable work in cinema came later with the 2010 film *Gohine Shobdo*, which earned him the prestigious Bangladesh National Film Award for Best Director. This recognition solidified his reputation in the Bangladeshi film industry. His next major project, *Jonakir Alo* (2014), was selected as Bangladesh’s official entry for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, though it did not receive a nomination. Despite this, the film marked another significant achievement in his career.

In addition to his work in film, Mithu was a talented painter. By 2004, he had held 11 solo exhibitions, showcasing his artistic talent and establishing himself as a respected figure in the visual arts. His ability to excel in both film and painting demonstrated his versatility and creativity.

Mithu was married to the painter Kanak Chanpa Chakma, and the couple had two children: a son, Arjo Srestha, and a daughter, Shiropa Purna. His personal life was as vibrant as his professional career, with his family and artistic endeavors playing significant roles.

Tragically, Mithu’s life was cut short on March 7, 2016, when a roadside tree collapsed onto the rickshaw he was traveling in, causing fatal injuries. The accident occurred in Dhanmondi Thana, Dhaka, and his sudden death was a great loss to both the Bangladeshi film and art communities.

Mithu’s legacy endures through his films, *Gohine Shobdo* and *Jonakir Alo*, as well as his contributions to painting. His work continues to be remembered and celebrated in Bangladesh, where he remains an influential figure in the arts. Despite his untimely death, his impact on cinema and visual arts remains significant, and his achievements continue to inspire future generations of artists and filmmakers.

title: Celâl Bayar
text:
Mahmut Celâlettin Bayar, better known as Celâl Bayar, was a prominent Turkish economist and politician who served as the third president of Turkey from 1950 to 1960 and previously as prime minister from 1937 to 1939. Born on May 16, 1883, in Umurbey, Bursa, he was the son of a religious leader and teacher who had emigrated from Ottoman Bulgaria. Bayar began his career working in banking and finance, eventually becoming a key figure in the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP), the political party that led the Young Turk Revolution. He played a significant role in organizing the CUP's branches in Izmir and Bursa and was involved in the 1913 Ottoman coup d'état. During the Turkish War of Independence, he supported the resistance against foreign occupation and participated in the Battle of Aydın. He was later elected to the Ottoman Parliament and served as a deputy for Saruhan (modern-day Manisa) and Izmir.

After the establishment of the Republic of Turkey, Bayar became a leading figure in the country's economic development. He founded İş Bankası, Turkey's first private bank, and played a crucial role in shaping the country's economic policies. As a member of the Republican People's Party (CHP), the sole legal party during the one-party period, he advocated for a blend of state intervention and private enterprise. In 1937, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk appointed him prime minister to implement liberal economic reforms, though his tenure was brief, ending in 1939 when he resigned due to disagreements with İsmet İnönü, Atatürk's successor.

In 1946, Bayar co-founded the Democrat Party (DP) with Adnan Menderes, Fuat Köprülü, and Refik Koraltan, marking the beginning of Turkey's multiparty system. The DP's platform emphasized political democratization, reduced bureaucracy, and economic liberalization while maintaining some elements of statism. The party's success in the 1950 elections led to a peaceful transfer of power, and Bayar was elected president. He was re-elected in 1954 and 1957, serving for a decade. During his presidency, Turkey aligned itself with the Western bloc, joining the Korean War in 1951 and NATO in 1952. Bayar also made the first official visit by a Turkish president to the United States in 1954.

Despite his moderate stance, Bayar's presidency saw significant social and economic changes. Inflationary policies encouraged private enterprise, and political participation expanded, particularly among Anatolians. However, the latter years of his presidency were marked by economic depression and increasing authoritarianism, culminating in the 1955 Istanbul Pogrom. His leadership was also characterized by a more partisan approach, as he publicly supported the DP during elections.

Bayar's presidency ended abruptly with the 1960 military coup. He was arrested and tried by the High Court of Justice on charges of treason and violating the constitution. Initially sentenced to death, his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. Despite two failed suicide attempts, he remained incarcerated until 1964, when he was released due to poor health. His release sparked protests, and he was briefly re-imprisoned before being freed permanently in November 1964. Bayar lived until the age of 103, passing away on August 22, 1986, after a brief illness. He remains one of the longest-lived former heads of state in history.

title: Rachel Weisz
text:
Rachel Weisz, an acclaimed English actress, was born on 7 March 1970 in Westminster, London, and grew up in Hampstead Garden Suburb. Her parents, George Weisz and Edith Ruth Teich, were immigrants to the UK from Hungary and Austria, respectively, fleeing the Nazis in 1938. Her mother converted to Judaism upon marriage, and Weisz’s maternal grandfather, Alexander Teich, was a Jewish activist. Weisz’s family valued the arts and encouraged independent thinking. She attended North London Collegiate School, Benenden School, and St Paul’s Girls School before studying English at Trinity Hall, Cambridge, where she graduated with upper second-class honours. While at university, she co-founded a drama group, Cambridge Talking Tongues, and won a Guardian Student Drama Award for an improvised play. She also trained under master clown Philippe Gaulier at École Philippe Gaulier.

Weisz’s acting career began in the early 1990s with television roles, including *Advocates II* and *Inspector Morse*. Her stage breakthrough came in 1994 with the revival of Noël Coward’s *Design for Living*, earning her a Critics’ Circle Theatre Award. Her film debut was in *Death Machine* (1994), followed by roles in *Chain Reaction* (1996) and *Stealing Beauty* (1996). She gained international recognition as Evelyn Carnahan in *The Mummy* (1999) and its sequel, *The Mummy Returns* (2001). During this period, she also appeared in *Suddenly Last Summer* (1999) at the Donmar Warehouse, earning critical praise.

In the 2000s, Weisz starred in several notable films, including *Enemy at the Gates* (2001), *About a Boy* (2002), and *Runaway Jury* (2003). Her performance as Tessa Quayle in *The Constant Gardener* (2005) earned her an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress, a Golden Globe, and a BAFTA Britannia Award. She also starred in *Constantine* (2005), *The Fountain* (2006), and *Agora* (2009), while winning a Laurence Olivier Award for her stage role in *A Streetcar Named Desire* (2009).

In the 2010s, Weisz continued to balance blockbusters and independent films, appearing in *The Bourne Legacy* (2012) and *Oz the Great and Powerful* (2013), as well as critically acclaimed works like *The Deep Blue Sea* (2011) and *The Favourite* (2018). For *The Favourite*, she won a BAFTA and received another Academy Award nomination. She also ventured into television with *Dead Ringers* (2023) and played Melina Vostokoff in *Black Widow* (2021).

Weisz’s personal life includes a past relationship with director Darren Aronofsky, with whom she has a son, and a marriage to actor Daniel Craig since 2011. They have a daughter together. She became a naturalised American citizen in 2011 and has been a brand ambassador for L’Oréal. Throughout her career, Weisz has been recognised for her versatility, earning multiple awards and critical acclaim across film, television, and theatre.

title: Michael Coulson (barrister)
text:
Michael Coulson was a British barrister, judge, and politician born on 23 November 1927 in the East Riding of Yorkshire, where his family had roots in Driffield. His father was a prosperous wool merchant, and Coulson attended the independent Fulneck School in Leeds before studying at Merton College, Oxford. He fulfilled his national service in the East Riding Yeomanry, part of Wenlock's Horse.

After completing his education, Coulson was called to the Bar by the Middle Temple in 1951 and joined the North Eastern Circuit, though he also practiced in London. He quickly gained a reputation for his exceptional memory, which he used effectively in his legal work. Around this time, he became involved in the Young Conservatives, helping to restructure the organization in northern England and even drafting their constitution. He also served in the Territorial Army, rising to the rank of Major in the Queen's Own Yorkshire Yeomanry.

In 1955, Coulson married Dilys Adair Jones, which brought him a 400-acre farm near Bolton Percy, North Yorkshire. Despite his enthusiasm for farming, he faced challenges, including a failed turkey farming venture during a harsh winter. The turkeys were eventually kept in the farmhouse airing cupboard for warmth, and the entire flock was later destroyed in a dispute with his father-in-law. Coulson also had a passion for horse riding and fox hunting, serving as secretary to meetings of the Bramham Moor and York and Ainsty Point to Point Races.

Coulson’s political career began with his election to Tadcaster Rural District Council, but he quickly aimed higher. In 1958, he was selected as the Conservative candidate for Kingston upon Hull North, a seat held by the Conservatives with a narrow majority. After an energetic campaign, he won the seat in the 1959 general election, increasing the majority to 702. His maiden speech in Parliament was noted for its wit and was reported in *Punch*. He supported Prime Ministers Harold Macmillan and Sir Alec Douglas-Home and was best known for successfully introducing a Private Member’s Bill to abolish the farthing as legal tender. In 1962, he became Parliamentary Private Secretary to the Solicitor General, Sir Peter Rawlinson, and was active in Commonwealth affairs as a member of the Conservative Commonwealth Council’s executive committee.

Coulson lost his parliamentary seat in the 1964 general election but soon advanced in his legal career. In 1965, he became an Assistant Recorder of Sheffield, and two years later, he was appointed Deputy Chairman of the Northern Agricultural Land Tribunal, a role he held for six years. From 1968, he also served as a Regional Chairman of Industrial Tribunals. His marriage to Dilys Adair Jones ended in strain, and in the 1970s, he relocated to the East Midlands to focus on chairing Industrial Tribunals full-time. He became a member of the Belvoir Hunt and, in 1977, married Barbara Chambers, a hunting acquaintance 20 years his junior.

In 1981, Coulson was appointed a Recorder of the Crown Court, and two years later, he became a Circuit Judge on the Midland and Oxford Circuit. Known in his home village of Wymondham, Leicestershire, as the "hunting Judge," he remained active in fox hunting and farming. In 1990, he received his final promotion as a Deputy Circuit Judge. One of his notable rulings came in 1994, when he awarded Trevor McAuley £5,900 in damages for unfair dismissal, including compensation for a campaign of mocking his Irish accent, setting a legal precedent. Coulson retired from the judiciary in 1998 at the age of 70 and died on 18 June 2002.

Throughout his career, Coulson combined his legal and judicial work with his interests in politics, farming, and hunting, leaving a mark in both the legal profession and his community.
